items.title: How North American freight rail makes money
items.body: Union Pacific keeps about 41 cents of operating profit from each revenue dollar because track is a fixed cost and prices rise faster than volume. That economics is why a reported US$85 billion Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern merger, with objections due at the US Surface Transportation Board on November 18, 2026, has CN and CPKC watching closely.
items.summary: Union Pacific turned each revenue dollar into about 41 cents of operating profit in Q3 2026 (computed). Here is how fixed track, pricing power and the operating ratio work, and why the UP-NS merger fight matters to CN and CPKC.
items.ai: Automation helps railroads in the places where cost is controllable: scheduling and train length, wayside inspection and maintenance planning, and back-office work. The sources read here do not quantify AI savings, so treat any such claim as unproven. One real signal: CN took a C$118 million impairment in Q3 2026 for discontinuing certain components of an IT project, a reminder that software spend can fail as well as pay. The physical network, not the software, is still what sets the cost base.
items.caseq: A Class I railroad's operating ratio has slipped 100 basis points in a year while revenue rose 15%, with fuel costs up about 60% and volume up 6%. The board asks whether the 'efficiency story' is broken. What do you recommend?
items.caseAnswer: Frame operating income as volume x revenue per unit x (1 - cost ratio), then separate what management controls from what it does not. 1) Decompose the ratio change: strip fuel first. Union Pacific said higher fuel prices cost about 140 basis points of operating ratio in Q3 2026 and CPKC said 170 basis points, so an unchanged or slightly worse ratio can hide better underlying cost control. Check fuel surcharge recovery, which lags. 2) Test price versus volume: UP's average revenue per car rose 8% while carloads rose 6%. If price is carrying growth, ask how much is mix (more low-yield intermodal) and how much is true like-for-like price above cost inflation. 3) Check network cost absorption: with a fixed network, extra volume should come at high incremental margins (UP's was about 41% on the Q3 revenue increase, computed). If incremental margin is below the average margin, look for congestion, crew shortages or overtime. 4) Check mix and cycle exposure: premium (intermodal) is half of UP's carloads but about a third of its freight revenue, so growth there dilutes revenue per car but needs little extra cost. 5) Recommend: report an ex-fuel operating ratio to the board, set incremental-margin targets by commodity group, protect investment in track and crews (rail peers spend around 17% of revenue on capex per AAR), and tie pricing to cost-to-serve rather than to the competitor's rate. Do not cut maintenance to flatter one year's ratio.

facts.k: Class I railroads, share of industry revenue

items.cs: Shippers, short lines and rival railroads are preparing evidence for the November 18 filings, and every one of them needs economic and network analysis. Investors and boards in trucking, ports and bulk commodities will want scenario work on rates, service and interchange if a transcontinental railroad is approved.

paras: A freight railroad is a toll road that also owns the trucks. It builds and maintains its own track, signals and yards, which cost roughly the same whether ten trains run or twelve, and then sells space on that network to shippers of grain, chemicals, coal, cars and containers. The business is therefore about two things: how much more it can charge each year, and how many extra cars it can push through track it has already paid for.

Union Pacific shows what that looks like when it works. In the third quarter of 2026 it reported revenue of US$7,197 million and operating income of US$2,943 million, according to its earnings release filed with the SEC. That is an operating margin of about 41% (computed), and an operating ratio, the share of revenue eaten by operating costs, of 59.1%. Few industrial companies earn that on a business that moves coal and corn.

The industry is also tightly held. The Association of American Railroads lists six Class I railroads in North America's freight network and says they take 93% of industry revenue, with about 635 short lines sharing the rest. Union Pacific, Norfolk Southern, BNSF and CSX are among them, as are CN and CPKC in Canada. That concentration is the backdrop to the proposed deal for Union Pacific to buy Norfolk Southern, which trade press reports at an enterprise value of US$85 billion and on which objections, protests and requests for conditions are due at the Surface Transportation Board on November 18, 2026, according to the STB's August 18 decision.
The rest of this piece explains where the margin comes from, why it moves the way it does, and why a rail merger is as much a story about price as about service.

Railroads sell a ton of freight moved over distance. The two headline unit measures are revenue per carload and revenue per revenue ton-mile, which is one ton carried one mile. CN reported freight revenue per revenue ton-mile of 7.70 cents in the third quarter of 2026, up 10%, and freight revenue per carload of C$3,353, up 15%, in its release filed with the SEC.

Revenue is grouped by what is shipped, and the groups behave very differently. Union Pacific splits its book into bulk (grain, coal, fertiliser), industrial (chemicals, metals, construction materials, forest products) and premium (intermodal containers and automobiles). In Q3 2026 premium handled 1,158,000 carloads, about half of the 2,293,000 total (computed), but earned US$1,889 per car, against US$4,004 for bulk and US$4,136 for industrial. Premium therefore made about 32% of freight revenue (computed from US$2,188 million of US$6,813 million) on half the cars.

That mix matters for two reasons. The revenue-per-car gap shows that the cheap-per-car traffic is the high-volume traffic. As analysis rather than a reported figure, intermodal competes with trucks on price, while heavy bulk freight has fewer alternatives over long distances.

The Canadian railroads sell a different basket. CPKC's third-quarter freight revenue was C$4,139 million, of which grain was C$904 million, up 29%, and intermodal C$815 million, up 22%, according to its Q3 release. CN's mix is heavier in petroleum and chemicals (C$1,000 million) and intermodal (C$1,065 million), with grain and fertilisers at C$923 million. Canadian rail leans on export bulk: grain, potash, coal and forest products moving to ports on both coasts.
Union Pacific's 2025 release quotes freight revenue excluding fuel surcharge, which rose 3% in 2025 on a 1% rise in revenue carloads, so price and mix did most of the work in that year.

Start with what a railroad spends. Union Pacific's Q3 2026 operating expenses were US$4,254 million. By line, compensation and benefits were US$1,264 million (about 30%, computed), fuel US$1,040 million (about 24%), purchased services and materials US$746 million (about 18%), depreciation US$643 million (about 15%), equipment rents US$206 million and other US$355 million, per the release. A year earlier fuel was only US$616 million, about 17% of costs (computed), so fuel is the one big line that swings with the oil market.

Most of the rest is fixed in the short run. Depreciation is the accounting shadow of a network that has to be rebuilt continuously: the AAR says US freight railroads spent about 17% of revenue on capital investment over 2016 to 2025, against around 3% historically for the average US manufacturer. CN planned a 2026 capital programme of about C$2.8 billion, and CPKC spent C$613 million on property additions in the third quarter alone. Crews are semi-fixed too, because a railroad cannot lay off and rehire locomotive engineers by the quarter.

Fixed cost explains the pattern of profit growth. When volume rises on a network that was not full, almost every extra dollar of revenue falls to the bottom line. Union Pacific's Q3 revenue rose US$953 million from a year earlier and operating income rose US$394 million, an incremental margin of about 41% (computed), even with a US$424 million jump in the fuel bill. That is why firm pricing and rising volume can lift profit faster than revenue.

Pricing is the other lever. Union Pacific's average revenue per car rose 8% to US$2,971 in the quarter while carloads rose 6%, so about half of the 15% freight revenue gain came from yield (computed from the release's figures). A railroad that raises rates above its own unit costs every year compounds the margin; one that cannot, because trucks or a rival railroad cap the rate, does not.

That ability is why regulators, and the filings now due at the STB, focus less on whether a merged railroad would run trains well and more on where shippers lose a competitive option. If a shipper can reach two railroads, the rate is disciplined. If it can reach one, the railroad has pricing power.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The operating ratio is operating expenses divided by revenue. Lower is better. A 59.1% ratio means 59.1 cents of every revenue dollar goes on running the railroad and 40.9 cents is operating profit (computed). Railroads report it every quarter, and it is the headline measure in each release read for this piece.

The ratio is a blunt tool, and the third quarter shows why. Union Pacific's reported ratio of 59.1% was 0.1 points better than a year earlier, but its adjusted ratio of 58.8% was 0.3 points worse. Management said higher fuel prices cost about 140 basis points of ratio; without fuel, the improvement would have been large. CPKC's reported ratio worsened 130 basis points to 64.8% and its core adjusted ratio worsened 120 basis points to 61.9%, with fuel responsible for 170 and 190 basis points respectively. CN's adjusted ratio improved 40 basis points to 61.0%, while its reported ratio worsened 230 basis points to 63.7% after the C$118 million IT impairment.

Because depreciation sits inside operating costs, a railroad that underinvests in track gets a better ratio today and a worse railroad tomorrow. And because the ratio is a percentage, a railroad can improve it by shedding low-margin freight that still contributes to fixed costs. That is a risk to watch rather than a reported finding.

Here is the counter-intuitive fact. In 2020, when the pandemic cut Union Pacific's carloads by 7% to 7,753,000 and revenue by 10% to US$19,533 million, the reported operating ratio improved, to 59.9% from 60.6% a year earlier, according to the company's fourth-quarter 2020 release. Lower fuel costs, down 38%, and cost cuts more than offset the fixed-cost penalty of lost volume. A downturn does not always show up in the ratio, so the number has to be read with the cycle and the fuel bill beside it.

Operating income still fell. It dropped US$720 million on a US$2,175 million fall in revenue, a decremental margin of about 33% (computed), lower than the 41% margin on the way up in Q3 2026, though the two periods differ in fuel and other conditions.

The biggest costs in the table above are labour, fuel and the network itself, and automation can reach each only partly. Better scheduling and train planning can raise asset use and reduce fuel burn. Wayside detectors and machine vision can turn inspections that used to be periodic into continuous monitoring, which matters in a business where a bearing failure stops a main line. Back-office work such as billing, customer service and crew management is the easiest to automate.

The sources read for this piece do not quantify any AI saving, so it would be a guess to put a number on one. What the filings do show is the cost of getting technology wrong: CN's C$118 million impairment came from discontinuing certain components of an IT project, and Union Pacific reported US$22 million of acquisition-related expense in the third quarter, a reminder that integration, not software, is the harder project in a rail merger.

The more durable effect may be on pricing and service data. Shippers who see real-time shipment status can compare railroads more easily, which helps the competitive end of the market, intermodal, and does little for captive bulk shippers. That is analysis, not a reported finding, and the next quarter's yield figures will show whether it is true.

The winners in this industry are railroads with dense networks, balanced traffic and the discipline to price above cost. Union Pacific's 59.1% ratio and 41% incremental margin are the benchmark in this group. The merger would join Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern into a single route of more than 50,000 route miles across 43 states, announced on July 29, 2025. Railpace reported terms of US$320 a share and an enterprise value of US$85 billion; these are trade-press figures, not read from the merger filings. Norfolk Southern's own ratio was not in the sources read.

The opposition is the part of the story due on November 18. According to Trucking & Transport News, CSX, BNSF, CPKC and Grand Trunk Railroad told the STB in early January 2026 that the application was incomplete and should be rejected. The STB accepted a revised application on May 28, 2026, paused it for more information, and in an August 18 decision restarted the clock without ruling on the merits. After November 18, applicants have until February 16, 2027 to respond, and a public hearing date is still to be set. Union Pacific's own target for the review runs into early 2027.

The Canadian angle: CPKC is among the objectors, and CN's release shows it is spending on the review, though it does not state a position, with C$14 million of advisory costs in Q3 and C$48 million year to date that it excludes from adjusted results.

For shippers and for the other railroads, the question is the same: does a combined railroad have more reason to keep a gateway open, or to keep traffic on its own line, where it earns the whole haul? That choice, repeated across thousands of origin-destination pairs, determines the toll. The evidence due on November 18 is mainly about it.

For anyone assessing the sector, the practical test is to look past the headline ratio. Read it ex-fuel, check price against volume, look at incremental margin by commodity group, and look at capital spending against revenue. A railroad that passes all four is earning its margin; one that passes only the first may be running down its network.

items.title: How Costco works
items.body: Costco sells goods at an 11.1% gross margin and still earned US$9.2 billion in fiscal 2026, because members pay US$5.9 billion a year for the right to shop. Half of its operating profit comes from the fee, not the merchandise.
items.summary: Costco's US$5.9 billion of membership fees equalled about half of its US$11.7 billion operating income in fiscal 2026 (computed). Here is how fees fund thin margins, why 92.3% renewal matters, how Kirkland Signature and Canada fit, and what could break it.
items.ai: AI touches Costco mostly at the edges: digitally-enabled sales grew more than 20% and management says traffic arriving from AI search is growing at triple-digit rates, but the warehouse model rests on few SKUs, bulk buying and low labour per dollar. The 10-K discusses AI mainly as a risk, notably for cybersecurity.
items.caseq: A membership warehouse club earns 11% gross margin, 9% SG&A and a fee equal to half its operating profit. A rival offers a free-shipping subscription at a lower fee. What do you recommend?
items.caseAnswer: Frame profit as members x fee x renewal, plus members x spend x thin merchandise margin, less SG&A. 1) Diagnose the profit pool: split operating income into the fee (US$5.9B) and the merchandise remainder (US$5.8B, computed) to see how much margin depends on renewal. 2) Test the threat on the right metric: renewal rate (92.3% in the U.S. and Canada, 89.8% worldwide), new-member sign-ups, and Executive upgrades (about half of paid members, computed), not headline fee comparisons. 3) Choose the response: do not cut the fee, because each point of price given away comes from a 2% net merchandise profit; instead widen the value gap through Kirkland Signature (at least 15% to 20% cheaper than national brands, per management), fuel and digital convenience. 4) Protect the base: hold SG&A near 9% of net sales, keep opening about 30 warehouses a year, and time any fee increase carefully. Prioritise by size and speed: first confirm renewal is intact, then raise perceived value, and use the fee lever last.

items.cs: Costco is a membership business that happens to sell goods at near-cost prices. Retailers, consumer-goods suppliers and private-equity investors will hire consultants to benchmark membership economics, private-label strategy and the pressure Costco's price position puts on rivals.

paras: Costco sells groceries, electronics, fuel and furniture at prices that leave it very little margin, and it makes the real money elsewhere. In the 52 weeks ended August 30, 2026 (fiscal 2026), the company reported net sales of US$297.2 billion, membership fee revenue of US$5.9 billion, operating income of US$11.7 billion and net income of US$9.2 billion, according to its fourth-quarter release. Divide the fee by operating income and you get about 50.6% (computed). Half of the profit, in other words, arrives before anyone has put anything in a trolley.

That is the answer to the master question of where the profit comes from. If Costco stopped selling a particular product tomorrow, the profit would barely move. If it lost its members, almost everything would. The merchandise is the reason people pay the fee and keep paying it; the fee is the reason the merchandise can be priced so thinly.

Run the 60-second test. Who pays? The member, once a year up front, and then again at the till. Is revenue recurring? Yes, in the sense that the fee renews annually, and 92.3% of members in the U.S. and Canada did so, according to the 10-K. Is there a locked-in consumable? No. The lock-in is cheap, bulk-sized value and the sunk cost of the fee. Who owns the assets? Costco is asset-heavy: it spent US$6.4 billion on capital expenditure in fiscal 2026 and plans about US$7.5 billion in fiscal 2027, per the 10-K. What would break it? The closing section sets out the candidates.

Costco has two engines and a few side streams. The first is membership. Fees are recognised evenly over the one-year membership term, so the US$5,907 million booked in fiscal 2026 reflects a pool built up over the year, with US$3,006 million of fees still deferred at year-end, according to the 10-K. The annual fee in the U.S. is US$65, which includes a free household card; fees vary elsewhere. Members can upgrade to Executive for an additional fee and earn a reward of generally 2% on qualified purchases, up to an annual cap the filing does not quantify here.

The second engine is merchandise. By the 10-K's sales mix, Foods and Sundries was US$116.8 billion (about 39.3% of net sales, computed), Non-Foods US$77.4 billion (26.0%), Warehouse Ancillary and Other Businesses, which includes fuel, pharmacy, food court and travel, US$61.4 billion (20.6%) and Fresh Foods US$41.7 billion (14.0%). Core merchandise sales rose 8% in the year while ancillary and other businesses rose 20%.

The side streams matter because they feed the same loop. Fuel is priced to draw visits. Digital sales, which Costco calls digitally-enabled, exceeded US$33 billion and grew more than 20% on the earnings call, with Uber Eats and DoorDash expanding delivery partnerships. Kirkland Signature, the house brand, is a private-label engine that carries a better margin than national brands while undercutting them on shelf price. These are not separate profit pools so much as reasons to renew.

In model-catalogue terms, Costco stacks a subscription (the fee), a loss-leader pricing policy (low markups to build trust), a private-label line and a float: deferred fees and fast inventory turns mean the company holds cash, ending the year with US$20.2 billion, per the release. Stacking those four is the point.

Start with merchandise. Net sales less merchandise costs left a gross margin of US$32,968 million, or 11.09% of net sales, according to the 10-K. Selling, general and administrative costs, which cover warehouse labour, rent and utilities, were US$27,190 million, or 9.15% of net sales. Subtract one from the other and the merchandise business produced about US$5,778 million before the fee, about 1.9% of net sales (computed). The fee of US$5,907 million then roughly doubles it, to the reported operating income of US$11,685 million.

The two margins people quote are therefore both right and answer different questions. Merchandise gross margin is 11.09% of net sales. Add the fees and the margin on total revenue of US$303,154 million becomes about 12.8% (computed), but SG&A is then about 9.0% of total revenue, the figure the release implies. The honest summary is that Costco runs on a gross margin in the low teens and an expense ratio near nine percent, which is why a fraction of a percentage point of mix matters so much.

Why can Costco run SG&A at 9% of sales? Because the warehouse is a very simple machine. The 10-K says a typical core warehouse carries fewer than 4,000 active items, against 9,000 to 11,000 online. Fewer items mean larger orders per supplier, fewer decisions, faster turns and less shrink. The company reports an average warehouse sales figure of US$292 million for fiscal 2026, against US$163 million in 2017, a rise that dilutes fixed costs.

The fee also hides a cost: the Executive reward. The 10-K says the reward, netted against sales, reduced net sales by US$3,383 million in fiscal 2026, which is about 57% of fee revenue (computed). Executive members are therefore partly paid back out of the fee they paid, and in return they spend a lot. The reward is a marketing expense dressed as a discount.

Finally, watch the noise. In the fourth quarter Costco received US$184 million from tariff refunds (US$174 million of refunds plus US$10 million of interest), a non-recurring benefit of US$0.15 per diluted share after partial reinvestment in member values, according to the earnings call and the release. One-off items like this make reported margin in a single quarter a noisy guide.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: It is the renewal rate. The 10-K reports 92.3% in the U.S. and Canada and 89.8% worldwide. Because the fee is half of operating income, a one-point change in renewal moves a chunk of profit. As an illustration, using the 84.1 million paid members and the roughly US$70 of fee revenue per paid member that falls out of the numbers (computed), one point of renewal is about 841,000 members and roughly US$59 million of annual fee revenue, before the spending those members would have done (computed).

The mix matters as much as the count. The 10-K reports 84.1 million paid members, up from 81.0 million, and 150.4 million cardholders including household cards. Of the paid members, 42.3 million, about 50% (computed), are Executive. According to the same filing, Executive members accounted for about 75.2% of worldwide net sales. Half the members and three-quarters of the sales: the people who pay the higher fee are also the heaviest shoppers, which makes the upgrade a self-selecting loyalty programme.

Fee increases are the second lever. The 10-K says the last U.S. and Canada increase, in September 2024, contributed about 30% of membership fee growth in fiscal 2026, so it has largely run through the numbers. The earnings call transcript, which is machine-assisted, has the CFO putting the effect at less than 1% of fee growth, so we treat the filing's 30% as the authority. A fee increase is a trust decision as much as a pricing one, which is why it is made rarely.
The pricing policy is what protects the renewal rate: Costco prices to keep members' trust rather than to extract the most from each basket, and the fee is the return on that restraint.

Costco's own filings describe AI mostly as an exposure. The 10-K cites it in several places, for example noting that the rapid evolution of AI has automated and accelerated the scale of cybersecurity threats. It does not quantify any AI savings.

Where AI shows up as an opportunity is the online channel. Management said on the earnings call that traffic from AI search grew at triple-digit rates for a second straight quarter and converts better than other traffic. That is a small part of a channel (digitally-enabled sales above US$33 billion, up more than 20%) that is itself a minority of a US$297 billion business.

The physical model limits automation. Few items, pallet-level handling and customers who do their own picking already strip out labour that other grocers spend on shelving and choice. The filing counts 355,000 employees, about 95% in warehouses and distribution, with 58,000 of them in Canada. Analysts should watch for automation in depots and online fulfilment, not in the warehouse floor, and for AI tools that compare Costco prices on the member's behalf and weaken the habit of simply going.

Costco's moat is scale combined with trust. The scale lets it buy fewer items in enormous volume; the trust lets it keep prices low without a fight over every receipt, because members have prepaid. Rivals can copy the shed, but copying the bargain is harder, because their own profit is in the markup and Costco's is in the fee.

Kirkland Signature is the clearest example of vertical logic. Management said on the earnings call that Kirkland items save members "at least 15% to 20%" against national brands, and it cut prices on several lines in the fourth quarter, such as walnuts from US$13.79 to US$9.99. The 10-K says the company expects to keep raising private-label penetration, though the sections we read gave no share-of-sales figure, so we do not state one. The same filing flags a risk: Kirkland quality and brand integrity matter, and it discloses class actions over Kirkland tequila labelling.

Canada is Costco's second-largest market and its best-performing by profitability. Canada had 115 of the 939 warehouses at year-end (about 12%, computed), 58,000 employees, and a segment revenue of US$40,561 million with operating income of US$2,107 million, per the 10-K. That is an operating margin of about 5.2% against about 3.5% in the U.S. and 4.5% in Other International (all computed from the segment table), and Canada produced about 18% of group operating income from about 13% of revenue (computed). Canadian comparable sales rose 7.8% in fiscal 2026 (6.7% excluding gasoline and currency), according to the Q4 release.

Expansion continues. Costco plans 33 openings in fiscal 2027, five of them in Canada, according to the earnings call. Retail Insider reports Canadian projects in Wasaga Beach, Lloydminster, East Windsor, Regina and Rocky View County due in late 2026, with Thunder Bay, Halton Hills, South Surrey and Oakville targeted for 2027, and Business Centres opened in New Westminster, B.C. in November 2025 and Winnipeg in March 2026. Timings are the developers' or Retail Insider's estimates, not Costco commitments. Costco says it is aiming for about 30 net new warehouses a year.

What could break it? First, trust: a clumsy fee increase or a visible drop in value would show up in renewal before it shows up in sales. Second, concentration: the 10-K flags reliance on the U.S. and Canada, and California alone is 26% of U.S. net sales. Third, cost: tariffs, inflation and the LIFO charge pressure margin even when refunds flatter a quarter. Fourth, competition and AI-driven shopping changes, which the filing names. Fifth, expansion: new warehouses can cannibalise old ones, as the 10-K itself warns. None of these is imminent, and the numbers are strong: fees up about 11% (computed from US$5,907 million against US$5,323 million) and paid members up 3.8% according to the earnings call. But a business that earns half its profit from a promise is only as strong as the promise.

items.title: The Ansoff matrix: four ways to grow
items.body: The Ansoff matrix sorts every growth idea into four boxes by whether the product and the market are old or new. Here is how it works, how consultants use it, and what it shows about Lululemon's latest results.
items.summary: Ansoff's four growth routes, ordered by risk and turned into choices, applied to Lululemon: Americas revenue down 8% in Q2 FY2026 while international grew 4%, men's at 24% of sales, and a new CEO arriving to reset the plan.
items.ai: AI is good at sorting a long list of growth ideas into quadrants, pulling market sizes and drafting the first economics for each; it cannot judge whether a firm's capabilities fit a move, or how much risk a board should carry.
items.caseq: A premium apparel brand's home market has stopped growing, but it is still profitable. The CEO asks how to restart growth. How would you structure the answer?
items.caseAnswer: Verdict: do not pick a quadrant first; list every idea, then test each against evidence. 1) Penetration: why has the core stalled? Check traffic, full-price sell-through, retention and competitor share before adding anything new. 2) Market development: which new countries, channels or customer segments could take the existing range, and what is the store, localisation and brand-building cost? 3) Product development: which new categories can the existing customer buy from the brand, and what would they cannibalise? 4) Diversification: is there any option worth a small, staged bet, or is it a distraction? For each idea size the prize, the capability gap and the time to revenue, then sequence: fix the core, scale the proven new market, pilot the next product, and treat diversification as an option with stop rules. Recommend a balanced portfolio with stage gates, and name the leading indicators for each quadrant.

facts.v: Penetration · Market dev. · Product dev. · Diversification

items.cs: Case-interview use: for any 'how do we grow?' question, sort ideas into the four quadrants, size each, test capability fit, and recommend a sequence with stop rules.

paras: Most growth conversations in a boardroom are really a pile of unrelated ideas: enter a new country, launch a new line, cut prices, buy a competitor. The Ansoff matrix is a way to sort that pile. It asks only two questions of any idea. Is the product something the company already sells, or something new to it? Is the customer or market one the company already serves, or a new one? Two questions with two answers each give four boxes, and each box carries a different kind of risk.

Igor Ansoff set this out in a 1957 Harvard Business Review article, "Strategies for Diversification". The Wikipedia entry on the matrix cites it as volume 35, issue 5, pages 113-124 (September-October 1957); we did not open the original. The four routes are market penetration (existing product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market), product development (new product, existing market) and diversification (new product, new market). Penetration means selling more of the same to the same people, through price, promotion, distribution or retention. Market development takes the existing range to new countries, channels or customer groups. Product development gives existing customers something new to buy. Diversification does both at once.

The matrix is popular with consultants because it is cheap and forces a choice of words. It will not tell you which idea is best. What it does is stop a team treating a new-country launch and a new-category launch as the same kind of risk, and it gives the discussion a common vocabulary before the numbers arrive. The sensible reading is the one a practitioner page at Umbrex gives: the grid is the beginning of strategy, and without customer evidence and economics it becomes "a slogan rather than a strategy".

Start by defining the two axes in one sentence each. A product is not a brand or a business unit; it is whatever the customer actually buys, at the level of detail that matters for capability. A market is a defined set of customers reachable through a defined set of channels. If the team cannot agree whether women's leggings sold to men are a new product or a new market, the matrix will produce an argument, not a decision. Umbrex lists vague definitions as the first pitfall, with teams misclassifying moves and debates going in circles.

Second, build a backlog of real ideas rather than filling the boxes with generalities. Each idea gets a one-line hypothesis and a quadrant. Ideas that straddle two quadrants should be split into pieces that can be tested separately: opening stores in a new country is market development, but launching a locally designed range there is product development layered on top.

Third, order by risk, but do it carefully. The usual ranking puts penetration lowest, market development and product development in the middle, and diversification highest, because each step away from the origin adds something the firm has not done before. Wikipedia's summary of the framework says exactly this and treats the two middle routes as similar in risk. Umbrex adds the necessary caveat: the risk gradient "generally increases" away from penetration, but it is not a law of nature and can mislead. A close segment next door can be safer than a complicated new product, and a penetration push into a hostile, price-war market can be riskier than it looks. Capability fit, industry structure and unit economics decide, not the box alone.

Fourth, test each idea on four things: the size of the prize (use a serviceable market, not a headline one), the capability gap (what the firm would have to build, buy or borrow), the economics (investment, time to revenue, cannibalisation of the existing business) and the evidence that customers want it. Umbrex's guidance is to keep a balanced portfolio, with most effort in penetration and near adjacencies and a small share in diversification. That 50-70% (penetration and near adjacencies) / 20-40% (product and market development) / 10-20% (diversification options) split is one practitioner's rule of thumb, not a law, but it captures the point that the core has to keep earning while the options are explored.

Lululemon is a useful test case because its latest numbers show all of the matrix's tensions at once. The figures below come from its second-quarter fiscal 2026 release (quarter ended 2 August 2026, published 3 September 2026), its fourth-quarter and full-year fiscal 2025 release (17 March 2026) and its fiscal 2025 annual report on Form 10-K (year ended 1 February 2026). All amounts are in US dollars.

Start with where the company sits. In fiscal 2025 the Americas generated US$7.847 billion of revenue, down 1.0% on the year, which was 71% of the total. China Mainland produced US$1.755 billion, up 28.9%, and the Rest of World (Asia-Pacific plus Europe, Middle East and Africa) US$1.501 billion, up 15.6%, according to the 10-K. Adding the last two gives international revenue of about US$3.256 billion, around 29% of the total (computed). International revenue grew by about US$596 million over fiscal 2024's US$2.660 billion, while the Americas shrank by about US$81 million (both computed from the 10-K). In other words, all of the company's net growth in fiscal 2025 came from outside the home region.

That is market development at work, and it is expensive in the way the framework predicts: it needs stores. The 10-K shows 811 company-operated stores at 1 February 2026, up 44 on the year, with 476 in the Americas, 172 in China Mainland (up from 151) and 163 in the Rest of World (up from 154). Mexico went from 17 stores to 26. Management said in the 10-K that it expects most 2026 openings to be in China Mainland, and the company also plans stores in new markets in Europe and Asia-Pacific. On the second-quarter call, management mentioned franchise stores in Athens and Bucharest and a Zalando marketing collaboration across 12 European markets, according to a call transcript published by Webull.

The second-quarter numbers show the limit of that route. Total revenue fell 4% to US$2.416 billion (down 5% in constant dollars), with the Americas down 8% and international up 4% (up 2% in constant dollars), according to Lululemon's release. China Mainland rose 4% as reported but fell 2% in constant currency, with comparable sales down 8% in constant currency. The Rest of World rose 5%. So the growth region slowed sharply at the same moment the core region weakened. Management blamed negative brand commentary and a different promotional calendar in China, according to the call transcript, which is reported speech rather than an audited fact.

Now the core, which is a penetration problem. Americas comparable sales fell 12% in the quarter. Management's stated priorities, per the transcript, are returning to full-price sales growth, cutting store SKU density by 15%, raising marketing in the second half and trimming pop-up shops from 65 to about 40. Those are classic penetration levers: reach, price realisation and retention in the existing market rather than new territory.

Product development is the third route. Men's was 24% of fiscal 2025 revenue and women's 63%, with accessories and other at 13%, according to the 10-K, which calls men's "a key pillar of our strategic growth plans". On the second-quarter call, men's revenue fell about 1%, leggings about 20% and accessories 13%, as reported by Webull's transcript. Whether men's is product development or market development is a fair argument, since it is both a new range and a new customer group, which is exactly why definitions matter. The new product chief appointed on 7 October 2026, Maggie Gauger, is to oversee design, merchandising, footwear and product innovation, according to the company's announcement. We found no footwear revenue figures in the sources we read, so we do not size that route.

On diversification, the sources we read show no active unrelated bet; the company's moves are all adjacent. The strategic reset is under way: interim co-CEOs ran the second quarter, new chief executive Heidi O'Neill was due to join the following week, and the company cut its fiscal 2026 revenue outlook to US$10.35-10.50 billion, a 5% to 7% decline, from earlier guidance of US$11.0-11.15 billion (just-style). The third-quarter outlook is for revenue down 10% to 11%. As of 16 November 2026 the third-quarter results had not been published.

A matrix is a classification, not a recommendation. The step that turns it into choices is a scored shortlist. Put each candidate idea in a row and give it the same columns: the prize in revenue and profit, the investment, the months to first revenue, the capability gap, the cannibalisation risk and the evidence so far. For Lululemon the shortlist might read: restore Americas full-price sales (penetration), keep opening in China and Europe (market development), grow men's and accessories (product development) and footwear (product development, size unknown). Each row then gets a different test.

Penetration is tested against the health of the core. If Americas comparable sales are down 12%, the question is whether the cause is product, price, brand sentiment or competition, because the fix differs. Adding new things to a broken core often just spreads the problem. Market development is tested on payback by market: the 172 stores in China Mainland produced US$1.755 billion, roughly US$10 million per store, against about US$16.5 million per store in the Americas (both computed crudely from the 10-K, since revenue includes online and store counts are year-end). That is a crude comparison that a consultant would refine with store-level data, but it frames the question of whether new-market stores earn their cost.

Product development is tested on cannibalisation and attach rates: does a new category bring new buyers, or only move existing ones around? Diversification, if on the list at all, is tested as an option: a small, time-limited pilot with explicit stop rules. Umbrex recommends managing the larger bets as options that scale with evidence, not all-or-nothing wagers.

Finally, sequence and own. The output of the exercise is a short list of two or three priorities, with an owner, a leading indicator and a review date for each quadrant. A good readout also states what the company will not do, which is where the matrix earns its keep: it makes a rejected idea easy to explain.

The most frequent error is sloppy definitions: classing a move in whichever box makes it sound safest. If an idea needs a new customer and a new product, call it diversification and price its risk that way. A related mistake is inflating the new market. A headline market size for a country or category is not what the firm can actually reach with its channels and brand, and Umbrex points to inflated market definitions as a reason new-market results disappoint.

Second, ignoring capability fit. Moving from selling online to running stores, or from clothing to footwear, calls for different skills in sourcing, fit, inventory and service. The matrix says nothing about whether the firm can do it. Third, forgetting that the boxes interact. A new product can cannibalise the core, and a new market can strain the supply chain that serves the old one. Lululemon's second-quarter inventory was US$1.711 billion, down 1% on the year, but units were down 7% (release), a reminder that more complexity in range and geography has to be carried in stock.

Fourth, penetration myopia: pushing the core harder with discounting. Lululemon's management said markdowns rose 70 basis points in the quarter (call transcript), and the general risk of discounting is real, because discounts buy volume at the cost of brand and margin. Finally, treating the matrix as the answer. It cannot tell a board whether the core is healthy, whether the economics work or whether the company can afford the bet. It simply stops the conversation from skipping those questions.

AI is most useful at the front and back of the process. At the front, it can take a long list of ideas from interviews, board papers and market reports, tag them to quadrants and flag the ones that straddle two. It can pull public numbers such as regional revenue, store counts and comparable sales from filings into a consistent table in minutes, and draft first-pass market sizing and unit economics with ranges. At the back, it can monitor the leading indicators for each quadrant and flag when one drifts.

The middle is where it is weak. Judging capability fit means knowing how an organisation actually works, such as whether its merchants can design a footwear range or whether its country managers can run franchise partners, and that knowledge is rarely written down. Choosing the acceptable level of risk is a decision about the owners' money and a board's patience. AI also reproduces whatever definitions it is given, so a muddled product or market definition will be sorted confidently into the wrong box. The practical rule is to use automation to widen the list and speed the numbers, then have people decide what is a product, what is a market and what the firm is prepared to lose.

items.title: How grocery retail makes money
items.body: Grocers sell perishable food that shoppers compare every week, so the profit left over is a few cents on the dollar. The levers are a point of gross margin, a pharmacy next door and a private label range.
items.summary: Loblaw earned a 6.9% operating margin in 2025, Metro a 4.8% adjusted net margin, and Empire about 2.3% (computed). Here is how Canadian grocers and Kroger turn thin margins into profit, why private label and pharmacy matter, and why two big automation write-downs show the limits of technology.
items.ai: Grocers use AI to forecast demand and cut spoilage, set prices and promotions by store, and plan delivery routes; none of it changes the thin margin structure, and automated fulfilment write-downs at Kroger and Empire show the risk of building fixed capacity ahead of volume.
items.caseq: A regional grocer's operating margin has fallen by one point while same-store sales grew 2%. What do you recommend?
items.caseAnswer: Frame profit as sales x (gross margin minus operating expense ratio). 1) Sales: traffic, basket size and price inflation, separating volume from price. 2) Gross margin: mix (fresh, pharmacy, health and beauty), private label penetration, supplier terms and promotional spend, and shrink. 3) Operating costs: labour scheduling, store and distribution productivity, rent and energy, and any under-used automation or e-commerce capacity. 4) Capital and risk: write-downs, capex returns and balance sheet. Quantify the one-point drop first, since a point of gross margin is a large share of a margin of a few percent, then prioritise private label and mix for durable gain and cost and capacity fixes for speed.

items.cs: Grocery is a high-volume, thin-margin business where a point of gross margin is a large share of profit. Scale, pharmacy and private label protect that point, and automation only helps where volume already justifies the fixed cost.

paras: A grocer buys food at a wholesale price, adds a markup, and sells it again within days. Most of what it sells is perishable, shoppers buy the same basket every week, and rivals' prices sit on the shelf for anyone to compare. That makes grocery a high-volume, low-margin business: profit is the thin gap between what a retailer earns above the cost of the food and what it spends running stores, trucks, warehouses and people.

The filings show how thin the gap is. Loblaw earned C$4,424 million of operating income on C$63,903 million of 2025 revenue, a 6.9% margin (computed), helped by a large pharmacy business. Metro's adjusted net earnings were 4.8% of sales. Empire, which owns Sobeys, made adjusted net earnings of C$747 million on C$31,950 million of fiscal 2026 sales, or 2.3% (computed). Kroger, the largest US supermarket group, reported an operating profit of $1.89 billion on $147.6 billion of sales, 1.3% (computed), and about 3.0% before a $2.5 billion impairment (computed). The question for any grocer is therefore not how to get rich but how to keep a few cents on each dollar while competitors watch every price.

Private label, meaning products sold under the retailer's own name, is the best-known way to improve that arithmetic, because the retailer keeps the margin that would otherwise go to a national brand. It is also hard to measure: the Loblaw and Metro results releases I reviewed give no private label sales figure, so the strongest claims about it rest on reasoning and on US data rather than on Canadian disclosure.

There are three engines. The first is food sold at a markup over its cost. The second is everything else on the same footprint, especially pharmacy, health and beauty, and in some banners fuel. The third is the retailer's own brands, which lift the margin on the food itself. At Loblaw in 2025, food retail sales were C$45,234 million (70.8% of revenue, computed) and drug retail sales C$18,669 million (29.2%, computed). Food same-store sales grew 2.3%. Loblaw also reported C$335 million of operating income from discontinued operations, which is its PC Financial business, and that sits outside the C$4,424 million above.

Gross margin, the share of sales left after the cost of goods, differs widely: Loblaw 31.3%, Empire 27.1%, Kroger 22.9% and Metro 19.9%. These are not a league table. Pharmacy, beauty, fuel and the way each company classifies costs all change the figure, so the useful comparison is each company against its own past. On that basis margins are edging up: Metro 19.9% from 19.7%, Empire 27.1% from 26.8% and Kroger 22.9% from 22.3%.

Private label works because the retailer commissions a manufacturer to make the product, skips most of the national advertising a brand would carry, and controls the shelf position. In the United States, the PLMA trade body, using Circana data, reports store brands at a 21.3% dollar share of 2025 sales, up from 19.1% in 2021, and a 23.5% unit share, up from 21.6%. Unit share above dollar share means store-brand items sell at a lower average price per unit (analysis, not a reported figure). Metro's release credits what it calls strong private labels but gives no numbers.

The point for a consultant is that private label is a bargaining tool as well as a margin tool. A credible own-brand alternative weakens a national supplier's demand for higher prices and gives the grocer a way to hold its price position when shoppers trade down.

Start with Loblaw's 2025 statement, all computed from its Q4 release. Cost of sales was C$43,871 million, 68.7% of revenue, leaving gross profit of C$20,032 million, or 31.3%. Selling, general and administrative expense was C$15,608 million, 24.4% of revenue, so it absorbed 77.9% of gross profit. Operating income was C$4,424 million, 6.9%. Loblaw's retail adjusted EBITDA margin, which excludes depreciation, was 11.2%.

Metro's structure is simpler and leaner. For fiscal 2025 on sales of C$22,006.7 million, gross margin was 19.9%, operating expenses 10.4% of sales, and operating income before depreciation and similar items C$2,082.9 million, or 9.5%. Adjusted net earnings were C$1,049.8 million, 4.8% of sales, and reported net earnings were 4.6%. Empire's adjusted EBITDA margin was 7.8% for fiscal 2026, against a reported 5.5% once a C$746 million e-commerce impairment is included.

The profit pool is broad and it is growing in dollars. The Competition Bureau's 2023 market study found that the three largest grocers' profits rose from C$2.4 billion in 2019 to C$3.6 billion in 2022, and that food gross margins rose one to two percentage points since 2017, which it called modest yet meaningful (as summarised by the law firm Fasken). The Retail Council of Canada, the industry lobby, argued to the Bureau that most of the gain came from pharmacy, health and beauty and from operating efficiencies, and that food margins were flat or down. That is a claim by an interested party, but it points at a real feature: the profit pool sits partly outside the food aisle.

Behind these margins is a mostly fixed cost base. Stores, distribution centres, leases and core staffing do not shrink when volume dips, so grocers earn their return on sales growth that outruns cost growth. Same-store sales rose 2.3% at Loblaw (food, 2025), 1.9% at Empire (fiscal 2026) and 1.6% at Metro in its fourth quarter, all nominal figures that include food price inflation.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The number is gross margin, measured in single percentage points of sales. Because the final profit is only a few cents on the dollar, a one-point move in gross margin is a large share of profit. At Metro, one point of sales is about 10.5% of its 9.5% EBITDA-style margin (computed). At Kroger, one point of sales is about $1.48 billion (computed), against operating profit before the impairment of roughly $4.4 billion (computed), a little over a third.

This explains the daily behaviour of grocers. Promotions, price matching and private label launches are all attempts to protect the number from two sides at once: shoppers who will switch store for a lower basket price, and suppliers who want to push through cost increases. It also explains why the number is political. The Competition Bureau's attention to margin gains since 2017 is a reminder that regulators and customers read the same figure grocers manage, and that a rise can be seen as the system working or as pricing power.

The partner number is the operating expense ratio. Metro held operating expenses at 10.4% of sales in both fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 while gross margin rose by 0.2 points, and its EBITDA-style margin moved from 9.4% to 9.5%. That is the operating leverage pattern in miniature: margin gains from mix and private label only reach profit if costs stay flat.

The most proven uses of AI in grocery are unglamorous: forecasting demand so fewer perishables are thrown out, setting prices and promotions by store and by item, and optimising delivery routes and shelf replenishment. They work on the two numbers above, either by protecting gross margin or by holding down operating expense. I found no filing that gives a dollar figure for the savings, so treat any consultant claim of a specific percentage as an assumption until a company discloses it.

The sourced evidence in the filings is about the opposite risk, automation that outruns volume. Kroger's 2025 operating profit fell to $1.89 billion from $3.85 billion in 2024, and its release attributes $2.5 billion of the decline to impairment and related charges on its automated fulfillment network, 1.7% of sales (computed). Empire's fiscal 2026 results include a C$746 million e-commerce impairment, 2.3% of sales (computed). In both cases the write-down arrived in a single year and was large enough to cut the reported margin visibly.

The lesson is that automating a fixed-cost asset raises the break-even volume. A highly automated warehouse is efficient at full utilisation and expensive at partial use, while a store-based pick model scales more gently. Grocers therefore gain most from AI that sits on top of existing stores and supply chains, and carry the most risk from AI that needs new assets and a sudden jump in online orders.

Canada is concentrated. The Competition Bureau called the industry highly concentrated and noted that at least eight large chains each had a different owner when the Competition Act was introduced in 1986, with five later bought by competitors. Loblaw, Sobeys and Metro each have over 1,000 stores, including franchised ones, and the Bureau reported their combined 2022 sales above C$100 billion. A USDA report, as cited by The Packer, puts shares at Loblaw 17%, Costco 15%, Sobeys 14%, Walmart 13% and Metro 6%, or 65% combined for the top five. That article does not state the data year, and its photo caption gives a different total of nearly 76%, so use these as an indication only. Costco and Walmart do not report Canadian sales separately.

Concentration helps explain the margin. Five chains that all see the same costs tend to move prices together without coordination, and the two price-led players, Costco and Walmart, are the main check on the others. Whoever has scale in purchasing, a pharmacy and health offer, and a trusted private label can defend gross margin; the regional or single-format grocer cannot.

On the cycle, grocery is a staple business and does not boom or bust with the economy. All three Canadian companies above kept growing same-store sales by 1.6% to 2.3%. The cycle shows up instead in mix. In the United States, store-brand unit share rose from 21.6% in 2021 to 23.5% in 2025, a period of high food inflation, which is consistent with shoppers trading down (analysis). Fresh food, pharmacy and private label are the segments that hold up; promotional national brands and discretionary general merchandise are where margin leaks.

The counter-intuitive fact is that a grocer's profit is not mainly decided in the food aisle. Loblaw's drug segment is 29.2% of revenue (computed), the Retail Council attributes much of the industry's margin gain to pharmacy, health and beauty, and the largest recent earnings shocks at Kroger and Empire came from automation write-downs, not from shoppers leaving. The winners combine a price reputation, a pharmacy that adds higher-margin sales, and a private label range that keeps the margin on the basket.

In a case interview you could say: grocery is a thin-margin, high-volume business where a point of gross margin is a third of profit, so it wins by building scale, a pharmacy and a private label range that protect that point, and by adding automation only where volume already justifies it.

items.title: How Dollarama works
items.body: Dollarama sells goods priced between 25 cents and five dollars from small stores that pay back in about two years, and it buys nearly half of its Canadian volume directly from overseas factories. That model produced a 26.7% operating margin in fiscal 2026.
items.summary: Dollarama earned C$1.31 billion on C$7.26 billion of sales in fiscal 2026, a net margin of about 18% (computed). Here is how direct import, a fixed price ladder and two-year store payback drive that margin, what Dollarcity and The Reject Shop add, and what could break it.
items.ai: AI and automation help Dollarama most in demand forecasting, replenishment and warehouse logistics, including a new Western Canada hub due by the end of 2027. They are a modest lever, because the main costs are goods and store labour, and the filings reviewed quantify no automation savings.
items.caseq: A Canadian dollar-store chain's EBITDA margin has fallen from 34.1% to 32.2% in a year as it adds an acquired foreign business. What do you recommend?
items.caseAnswer: Frame profit as store count x sales per store x margin, less overhead. 1) Diagnose the mix: separate the core Canadian segment (45.7% gross margin, 34.9% EBITDA margin) from the acquired Australian one (about 5.5% EBITDA margin, computed) to confirm the decline is mix, not core erosion. 2) Core health: check comparable sales (transactions versus basket), imported cost, freight and currency pass-through, and private-label share. 3) Acquired business: set a timeline to lift gross margin and cut SG&A through sourcing, store layout and range changes, and stop new openings if renovated stores do not beat the old ones. 4) Capital allocation: keep new Canadian stores (about two-year payback) and the Latin American stake ahead of buybacks and the foreign turnaround if cash is tight, and watch leverage (2.12x adjusted net debt to EBITDA). Prioritise by size and speed: confirm the mix explanation first, then fix Australia's cost base, while protecting the Canadian engine.

facts.k: Direct imports, share of Canadian volume

items.cs: Dollarama is a low-price, high-turnover retailer whose margin comes from direct import, private label and cheap stores that pay back in about two years. The winners in this format are the chains with the scale to buy cheaper than rivals and the store economics to keep opening more.

paras: Dollarama sells everyday goods, seasonal items and consumables at a fixed set of low prices, and it has turned that simple idea into one of the most profitable retail formats in Canada. In the year ended February 1, 2026, it reported sales of C$7,255.8 million, EBITDA of C$2,408.2 million (a 33.2% margin) and net earnings of C$1,309.4 million, which is about 18.0% of sales (computed). Most grocers and general merchants dream of an operating margin in the single digits. Dollarama reported 26.7%.

The master question is where the profit comes from. The answer is not one product. It is a loop: buy a large share of the range directly from factories overseas, price it at a few round numbers, put it in small, cheap-to-run stores, and let frequent low-ticket visits fill those stores. Cheap goods bring traffic, traffic fills the stores, full stores pay back quickly, and quick payback funds the next store.

Under the 60-second test, the customer pays at the till, once per visit, for a basket of low-priced goods. Revenue is repeat rather than contractual: there is no subscription and no consumable lock-in, so loyalty comes from habit and price. Dollarama owns its distribution network and buys its goods, so it is asset-heavy in logistics but mostly leases its stores. What would break it is covered at the end.

There are three engines. The first and largest is Canada, with 1,734 stores at the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (13 weeks ended August 2, 2026). The second is Dollarcity, a Latin American dollar-store chain in which Dollarama holds equity-accounted stakes, so it contributes earnings but not sales. The third is Australia, where Dollarama bought The Reject Shop in July 2025 and now runs 414 stores. Consolidated second-quarter sales were C$2,026.6 million, up 17.6%, helped by the Australian addition.

Canadian pricing is a ladder. According to the 2026 Annual Information Form, items range from C$0.25 up to C$5.00. Dollarcity's range is US$0.69 to US$4.00, and Australia's is A$0.45 to A$15.00. The ladder matters because it lets management trade up the basket, for example by selling a C$4 or C$5 item that would once have sat in a department store, without losing the identity of a low-price shop. The Form says seasonal products were about 13% of Canadian sales in fiscal 2026, which gives a steady flow of reasons to visit.

The mix is also protective. The Form states that 65% of Canadian sales came from private label and 35% from national brands. Private label carries a better margin and cannot be price-compared in a rival store, because the same item does not exist there.

Dollarcity is the quiet profit engine. Dollarama's share of Dollarcity's net earnings for calendar 2025 was C$191.5 million, up 47.4%. That equals about 14.6% of Dollarama's fiscal 2026 net earnings (computed, though the periods differ by a month). Dollarcity had 781 stores on June 30, 2026, against 658 a year earlier, and its sales grew 30.0% in the second quarter. Dollarama holds 60.1% of the main operating company (CARS) and 80.05% of ICM, the entity expanding in Mexico.

Start with the income statement for fiscal 2026: gross margin 45.0%, selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expense 15.1% of sales, EBITDA margin 33.2% and operating margin 26.7%. Capital spending was only C$272.8 million, about 3.8% of sales (computed). A business that earns a 33% EBITDA margin and spends under 4% of sales on capex converts a large share of earnings to cash. That is the profile of a very good retailer.

The source of the gross margin is direct import. The Form says 46% of Canadian procurement volume in fiscal 2026 was overseas direct imports, from more than 25 countries, with the vast majority from China. The other 54% came from North American vendors. Buying direct removes the wholesaler's margin and lets Dollarama specify the product and the pack size. Concentration risk is modest: the largest vendor is about 6.2% of Canadian purchases and the top ten about 35%.

The store economics explain the growth plan. Per the Form, a new Canadian store needs about C$1 million of capital and inventory, net of tenant allowance, and pays back in about two years. New stores are expected to sell more than C$3.2 million in their first two years, and the average store sells about C$4.1 million. On an average footprint of 10,455 square feet, that is roughly C$392 per square foot (computed). Management targets about 2,200 Canadian stores by 2034, which is about 466 more than today's 1,734 (computed). Guidance for fiscal 2027 calls for 65 to 75 net new Canadian stores.

The margin did slip in the most recent quarter, and the cause is mix rather than the Canadian engine. Second-quarter consolidated gross margin was 44.5% against 45.5% a year earlier, and SG&A rose to 15.1% from 14.0%, which pushed EBITDA margin down to 32.2% from 34.1%. Canada alone had a 45.7% gross margin and a 34.9% EBITDA margin. Australia reported a 32.4% gross margin, SG&A at 28.1% of sales, EBITDA of C$10.2 million on C$184.8 million of sales (about 5.5%, computed) and an operating loss of C$17.1 million. Australia reduced diluted earnings per share by C$0.05 in the quarter, and management still expects a net loss there for fiscal 2027.

The Australian purchase shows the trade-off. The Reject Shop was bought for A$233.6 million, from an offer of A$6.68 a share, according to the Form. It brings a second large market and a store base, but at a fraction of Canadian profitability for now. Dollarama is refitting stores, with 60 using its layout and fixtures, while keeping the old banner until the range better reflects its value offer.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The number is comparable store sales in Canada, because it tells you whether the existing store base is getting more productive. Fiscal 2026 comparable sales rose 4.2%, and the second quarter of fiscal 2027 rose 5.4%, made up of 3.7% more transactions and a 1.7% larger average basket. Growth in transactions is the healthier half: it means more people are visiting, not just paying more per visit. In September 2026, management raised its fiscal 2027 comparable sales guidance to 4.0% to 4.5% from 3.0% to 4.0%.

Why does this one figure matter so much? Because the cost base is largely fixed once a store opens, in the form of rent, staff and lighting. Extra sales on the same space flow to profit at a high rate. It also validates the payback maths: a store that grows its sales after the two-year ramp is a better investment than the initial model assumed.

Watch two companions. The first is gross margin in Canada, guided at 45.0% to 45.5% for fiscal 2027, because that shows whether imported costs, freight and currency are being passed through. The second is net new stores, because comparable sales exclude them and the growth story needs both. A company opening 65 to 75 stores a year on a base of 1,734 is adding about 4% to its store count (computed).

Retail automation lands in places where Dollarama is already structurally strong. Demand forecasting and replenishment matter for a chain with thousands of low-priced items and a large seasonal range, because an overstocked item at a low price point has little room for markdown. Assortment and pricing tools can help management decide which products justify a C$4 or C$5 slot on the ladder.

Logistics is the other area. Dollarama says it operates seven warehouses and one distribution centre in Canada, with a Western Canada hub near Calgary due by the end of calendar 2027. That project is the main reason capital spending is guided at C$420 million to C$470 million for fiscal 2027, against C$272.8 million in fiscal 2026. Automated sorting and routing are typical in such facilities, though the company's filings that I reviewed do not quantify any automation savings, so this is a reasoned expectation, not a reported result.

The honest view is that AI is a modest lever here. The costs that matter most are the goods and the store labour, and the customer's trip to a physical shop cannot be replaced by software. Online shopping is not a significant disclosed line in the figures reviewed, which suggests the store remains the engine. The more relevant technology threat is indirect: online marketplaces selling similar imported goods at low prices, which is a pricing risk rather than an automation one.

Dollarama wins on cost and scale, not on network effects or switching costs. The moat checklist is clear. Scale and cost advantage are the real ones: direct sourcing from overseas factories, a distribution network that serves more than 1,700 Canadian stores, and a store model that pays back in about two years. A rival with fewer stores buys in smaller volumes and carries higher unit costs. Brand is a secondary moat, since the name stands for low prices to Canadian shoppers. Switching costs are close to zero, so the moat depends on staying cheaper and more convenient than the alternatives.

The competition looks fragmented and small next to it. The Form names Dollar Tree Canada, Your Dollar Store With More, Great Canadian Dollar Store and Buck or Two Plus! as pure-play dollar chains, with about 500 stores between them (Dollarama's own estimate). Dollarama's 1,734 Canadian stores are more than three times that figure (computed). The larger threat is from general merchants and grocers such as Walmart, which can discount many of the same categories as part of a bigger trip. That comparison is my own judgement, not a figure from the filings, but it explains why Dollarama keeps adding consumables and keeps its prices low: it competes for the everyday basket, not just the occasional impulse item.

Capital allocation is disciplined and returns cash. In fiscal 2026 the company repurchased 4,426,267 shares for C$834.2 million at an average of C$188.47. That equals about 63.7% of fiscal 2026 net earnings (computed). In the second quarter of fiscal 2027 it bought another 1,596,016 shares for C$300.4 million. The current normal course issuer bid allows up to 13,532,086 shares, or 5.0% of those outstanding. The quarterly dividend was raised 13.4% to C$0.12 a share. Net debt was C$2,517.0 million at the end of the second quarter, or 2.12 times adjusted EBITDA, which is moderate and sits within a business that funds growth and buybacks from cash flow, with new notes issued in 2026 to refinance.

What would break it? Five things deserve attention. First, tariffs, freight and currency changes, because 46% of Canadian purchase volume is imported and most of it from China. Second, comparable sales turning negative, which would expose the fixed cost base. Third, a saturated Canadian market, since the 2,200-store target implies only about 466 more locations. Fourth, Australia consuming management time and capital without reaching Canadian returns, with a net loss still expected for fiscal 2027. Fifth, valuation: the company buys back shares at prices near C$188, so poor returns on that spending would be a self-inflicted loss.

In a case interview you could say: Dollarama is a low-price, high-turnover retailer that earns a 33% EBITDA margin because it imports roughly half of what it sells, runs cheap stores that pay back in about two years, and funds expansion and buybacks from cash flow, so it stays ahead as long as it keeps costs below those of rivals and customers keep coming back.
