items.title: Unit economics: knowing what one customer is worth
items.body: Unit economics compares what a customer is worth with what it cost to win them. Here are CAC, LTV and payback, applied to Duolingo's latest filing, with every figure sourced or labelled.
items.summary: CAC, churn, LTV, payback and LTV:CAC explained with a small assumption-based example, then applied to Duolingo's Q3 2026 results: 13.1 million paid subscribers, 72.9% gross margin, and why public data can only bound its true CAC.
items.ai: AI is good at assembling cohort tables and sensitivity runs from filings and event data, but it cannot choose which churn or CAC figure to trust, or decide how much growth a firm should buy.
items.caseq: A subscription app spends $20 million a year on marketing and adds 400,000 paying customers. Is the business healthy, and what would you check?
items.caseAnswer: Verdict: cannot say yet; the figures give a blended CAC of $50 (computed: 20 million / 400,000), so the answer depends on four checks. 1) Revenue: price per customer and plan mix. 2) Cost to serve: gross margin and contribution margin after fees and support. 3) Retention: monthly churn by cohort, which sets lifetime and LTV. 4) Acquisition: paid versus organic split and marginal CAC by channel. Then compute gross-margin-adjusted LTV and payback, compare with cash available to fund growth, and treat any benchmark ratio as a sense check only. Recommend scaling the channels where payback is short and cohorts hold, and fixing retention before buying more users.
cheat: CAC is the full sales and marketing cost of winning one new customer.
LTV is expected lifetime revenue per customer; adjust it by gross margin for a truer value.
Lifetime in months is roughly 1 divided by monthly churn (a simplification).
Payback = CAC divided by monthly gross profit per customer.
LTV:CAC above 3 is a typical software guideline (Skok), not a recommendation.
Use cohorts and marginal CAC; blended averages hide weak channels.
Duolingo Q3 2026: 13.1M paid subscribers, 72.9% gross margin, S&M $42.2M.
Duolingo does not disclose CAC or churn, so any ratio for it is an estimate.

facts.v: Value of one customer vs cost to win

items.cs: Case-interview use: for any customer-growth question, compute gross-profit LTV, CAC and payback, then check churn by cohort before judging growth spend.

paras: Unit economics asks a plain question: for one customer, how much money comes in, how much it costs to win and serve them, and how long until the account pays for itself. A business can grow fast and still lose money on every customer. A business can also look small and be very healthy if each customer is worth far more than it cost to find. The framework turns that into a handful of numbers a team can track and argue about.

The terms are short. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is the sales and marketing spend needed to win one new customer. Churn is the share of customers who leave in a period. LTV (lifetime value) is the total revenue a customer is expected to bring before leaving. Gross-margin-adjusted LTV counts only the gross profit from that revenue, after the direct cost of serving the customer. Payback period is the time it takes for a customer's gross profit to repay the CAC. LTV:CAC is lifetime value divided by acquisition cost. Contribution margin is what is left of revenue after all variable costs, including those of serving, collecting and supporting the customer, but before fixed overheads.

The master question for this piece is: why would this business still be winning in ten years? Unit economics answers a narrow part of it. It shows whether each new customer adds to the firm's value or drains it, and which lever (price, retention, cost to serve or cost to win) matters most. It does not show whether customers will still want the product in ten years, which is a question about moat and demand.

Start with the customer definition. A customer must mean the same thing in the numerator and the denominator. Count paying customers, not sign-ups, unless free users are part of the funnel you are pricing. Split the analysis by segment, channel or cohort (customers who joined in the same month), because an average across very different groups hides the answer. A cheap channel that brings in short-lived customers can look good on CAC and bad on LTV.

Next, measure CAC fully. Include the salaries of the sales and marketing team, advertising, tools and agency fees, not only media spend. Use spend from the period before the customers arrived if sales cycles are long. Separate paid CAC from blended CAC: blended CAC divides all spend by all new customers, including those who came through word of mouth, so it flatters the paid channels. Most public companies report only total sales and marketing expense, which means an outsider can only compute rough proxies, not the company's own CAC.

Then estimate LTV. The standard shortcut is monthly revenue per customer, multiplied by gross margin, divided by monthly churn. The logic is that expected lifetime in months is about one divided by the monthly churn rate. Two cautions follow. First, use gross margin, not revenue, otherwise a low-margin business looks richer than it is. Second, churn is an estimate that can move a lot: an essay on LTV by Jason Cohen (A Smart Bear) argues LTV is not a stable, knowable number and can change by roughly 2x within a year, and that it should not be used alone to set acquisition spending.

Finally, compute payback: CAC divided by monthly gross profit per customer. Payback is more robust than LTV because it needs no forecast beyond the first months, and it speaks directly to cash. A firm with long payback has to fund growth with capital; a firm with short payback can recycle cash into acquisition. Contribution margin belongs here too: if support, payment fees or delivery costs vary with each customer, subtract them, otherwise payback is understated.

Benchmarks help you ask whether your numbers look odd, but they are not goals. David Skok, a venture investor, wrote that a guideline for a successful software-as-a-service business is that LTV:CAC should be higher than 3, and that this assumes the simpler LTV formula and a gross margin of 80% or higher (typical guideline, published by a VC, not a rule). He also notes that his under-12-months guideline for recovering CAC was written in 2011 and is dated, and that enterprise land-and-expand models can run around 20 months. Cohen's essay reports the common view that 3 is healthy and 5 very good, but questions the approach. The ratio of 3 is a rule of thumb for a certain kind of subscription software with high gross margin. It does not tell a consumer app, a marketplace or a hardware seller what to target.

First, a small illustration. Every number in this block is an ASSUMPTION for teaching, not data from any company. Suppose a subscription costs $10 a month, and serving it costs $2 a month, so gross margin is 80% (assumption). Suppose card fees and support cost another $1 a month per customer, so contribution margin is $7 a month, or 70% of revenue (assumption). Suppose monthly churn is 5%, so expected lifetime is 1 / 0.05 = 20 months (computed from the assumption). Simple LTV is $10 x 20 = $200. Gross-margin-adjusted LTV is $8 x 20 = $160. If CAC is $50 (assumption), LTV:CAC on the adjusted figure is 160 / 50 = 3.2, and payback is $50 / $8 = about 6 months (computed). Change churn to 8% and lifetime falls to 12.5 months, adjusted LTV to $100, and the ratio to 2.0, with no change in marketing at all. That sensitivity is the point of the exercise.

Now a real company: Duolingo, the language-learning app. It is a useful case because it reports paid subscribers, daily users, gross margin and sales and marketing expense every quarter, and because most of its users are free. Its figures come from its third-quarter 2026 shareholder letter, filed with the SEC. In that quarter it reported total revenue of $309.0 million, of which $270.0 million was subscription revenue, against $271.7 million and $229.5 million a year earlier. Paid subscribers at the end of the quarter were 13.1 million, up from 11.5 million. Daily active users were 64.9 million and monthly active users 153.1 million. Gross profit was $225.1 million, a gross margin of 72.9%, up from 72.5%. GAAP sales and marketing expense was $42.2 million, against $35.1 million a year earlier.

What can an outsider compute? Sales and marketing was about 13.6% of revenue (computed: 42.2 / 309.0). Paid subscribers were about 8.6% of monthly active users (computed: 13.1 / 153.1), which shows the funnel: most of the 153.1 million users pay nothing, and the free tier is both a product and an acquisition channel. Subscription revenue per period-end paid subscriber was about $20.6 for the quarter, or about $6.9 a month (computed: 270.0 / 13.1, divided by three; this ignores that subscribers changed during the quarter, and that subscription revenue includes some plan types with different prices). Applying the company-wide gross margin of 72.9% gives about $5.0 of gross profit per subscriber per month (computed; the margin is for the whole company, not only subscriptions).

Duolingo does not disclose CAC, subscriber churn or retention in the letter, so a true LTV:CAC cannot be computed from public data. We can, however, run a deliberately harsh test. Net paid subscriber additions over the year were 1.6 million (computed: 13.1 - 11.5). If we assume the third-quarter sales and marketing figure repeats in each of four quarters, annual spend is about $169 million (est., computed: 4 x 42.2), and dividing by net additions gives about $105 per net new subscriber (computed). At $5.0 of monthly gross profit, that implies payback of about 21 months (computed). This is an upper bound and not Duolingo's CAC: net additions are lower than gross additions because some subscribers leave, the spending also supports free users and retention of existing users, and all of it is annualised from one quarter. The real figure is likely lower.

The same filing contains a clue about where the company is pointing the lever. Daily users rose to 64.9 million from 50.5 million, about 29% (computed), faster than paid subscribers, which rose about 14% (computed). Duolingo says it ran experiments aimed at increasing user retention and DAUs. The reading, an inference and not a company statement, is that growing free daily use feeds the paid funnel more cheaply than buying new users.

A set of unit-economics numbers is only useful if it changes a decision. There are four levers: raise price or revenue per customer, cut the cost to serve, lower CAC, or lengthen customer life by reducing churn. Test each against the others. A 1-point cut in monthly churn often beats a 10% cut in CAC, because it lifts LTV for every customer already won, while a CAC cut helps only future ones. The worked illustration above shows this: moving churn from 5% to 8% cut the ratio from 3.2 to 2.0.

Next, decide how fast to spend. If payback is short and the cohort is reliable, spending more on acquisition grows value, until the marginal customer (the next one, from a costlier channel) pays back too slowly. Average CAC is not marginal CAC. A company should compare channels at the margin and stop where payback exceeds what it can fund or how long it expects customers to stay.

For Duolingo, the choice visible in the data is the free-to-paid funnel. With paid subscribers at roughly 8.6% of monthly users (computed), a small improvement in conversion adds many paying customers at almost no extra acquisition cost, and daily habit is the likely driver of that conversion. That is an inference from the company's stated focus on retention and DAUs, not a company statement about its own conversion economics. The choice for management is how much to push monetisation (which can annoy free users) against engagement (which feeds future conversion).

For an investor or consultant, the next step is to ask for what is missing: subscriber churn by cohort, gross additions, and split of S&M between acquiring users and retaining them. Without them, any LTV:CAC figure for a public company is an estimate, and should be labelled as one. A recommendation built on a benchmark alone, such as 'raise spending until the ratio falls to 3', mixes up a rule of thumb with a decision.

The first mistake is using revenue instead of gross profit. A customer who brings $200 of revenue and $100 of cost is not worth $200. The second is using blended CAC, which includes free word-of-mouth growth, to judge a paid channel; the marginal customer costs more than the average one.

The third is relying on a single churn number. Churn is rarely flat: new customers often leave faster than old ones, and a monthly figure taken from a growing business mixes young and old cohorts. Cohort curves are more honest. The fourth is treating LTV as a precise forecast. As noted above, it can move by a large factor in a year, which makes LTV:CAC a rough signal.

The fifth is applying a benchmark as a target. A ratio of 3 or a payback of 12 months came from software businesses with high margins and, in Skok's own account, the payback guideline dates from 2011. A firm with strong cash, long customer life and lower margin may rationally accept a different number, and one with weak cash may need much shorter payback than any guideline says.

The sixth is leaving out costs and time. Contribution margin should include payment fees, support and discounts, and cash timing matters: annual plans paid up front change payback. Finally, do not mix labels. When a public company does not give CAC, say so, label your proxy as computed and say what it overstates or understates.

AI helps most with the measurement work. It can pull subscriber counts, margins and marketing expense from filings into a consistent table, rebuild cohorts from raw event data, and flag when a segment's churn drifts. It can also run sensitivity tables in seconds, which makes the point about churn and price easy to see.

AI also changes the inputs. In consumer apps, generative features can raise the cost to serve, because each active user triggers computing costs, which pushes gross margin down; the Duolingo letter shows gross margin at 72.9%, so it is worth watching whether that holds as usage rises. Automation can lower CAC through better targeting and lifecycle messaging, and lower support costs. But if every competitor uses the same tools, the gain in CAC is competed away, so the lasting advantage lies in retention and product, not in the ad machine.

What AI cannot do is decide which number to trust. It will fill a gap with a plausible churn rate or a neat ratio, so every figure must be checked against a filing or labelled as an assumption. It also cannot judge whether spending more on growth is wise given a company's cash and strategy. That is a human decision about risk.

In an interview: unit economics compares what one customer is worth, in gross profit over their life, with what it costs to win them, and a business is healthy when payback is quick and retention is strong, whatever any rule-of-thumb ratio says.

items.title: How airlines make money
items.body: Airlines sell a perishable seat on a machine that costs almost the same to fly full or empty, so profit comes from a few points of load factor, a premium cabin and a loyalty programme. In 2026 a fuel shock showed how thin that margin really is.
items.summary: The world's airlines will earn about 2% net margin on $1.17 trillion of revenue in 2026, roughly $4.50 per passenger, according to IATA. Here is where the money comes from at Air Canada and Delta, why fuel and labour take more than half the bill, and why the best airlines are partly banks and partly premium-cabin sellers.
items.ai: Airlines use AI and automation in revenue management (pricing every seat by the hour), crew and aircraft scheduling around disruption, predictive maintenance and airport self-service, but none of it removes the two big costs, fuel and people.
items.caseq: An airline's net margin has fallen from about 4% to 2% in a year, driven by jet fuel. What do you recommend to restore profit?
items.caseAnswer: Frame profit as (revenue per seat-mile minus cost per seat-mile) x seat-miles flown. 1) Revenue: yield (fares, premium cabins, ancillaries and fuel surcharges), load factor, and non-ticket income such as loyalty and cargo. 2) Cost: fuel (hedging, fleet efficiency, pass-through), labour (productivity, contracts), ownership (leases, aircraft age) and airport and other fees. 3) Capacity: cut or redeploy the least profitable routes and cap growth while rivals face the same fuel price. 4) Balance sheet: liquidity, sale-leasebacks and government support to survive the trough. Prioritise by size and speed: pass-through and capacity discipline first, loyalty and premium mix as the durable lever.
cheat: IATA forecasts 2026 industry revenue of $1.165T and net profit of $23.0B, a 2.0% net margin, about $4.50 per passenger (IATA, 7 Jun 2026).
Fuel is 31.4% of industry operating costs in 2026, up from 25.4% in 2025; labour is $271B, about 24% of costs (computed).
At Air Canada in 2025, wages (23.3%) and fuel (22.1%) were the two biggest costs, each computed from the annual report (22,372 revenue, 21,454 costs).
Air Canada Q3 2026: revenue C$6,984M, operating margin 3.7%, fuel bill up C$906M year on year.
Delta, Q2 2026: premium tickets (35.0%) edged out main-cabin tickets (34.7%) as a share of revenue (computed).
Delta collected $2.4B from American Express in one quarter, a loyalty income stream that behaves like a bank, not a seat sale.
Air Canada and WestJet together carry up to 78% of domestic traffic on key routes (Competition Bureau, via C2C Journal).
Counter-intuitive: the industry has never posted a net margin above 5%, and its ROIC (4.3%) sits below its cost of capital (8.5%).
items.cs: Airlines are a high-fixed-cost, near-commodity business where the margin ceiling is set by fuel, labour and aircraft supply. The winners are the carriers that fill planes, sell premium seats and turn their loyalty programme into a second business.

paras: An airline sells a seat on a specific flight, and once the door closes an empty seat is worth nothing. The aircraft, the pilots, the fuel to get airborne and the landing fees are nearly the same whether the plane carries 120 people or 180. That makes airlines a fixed-cost, perishable-inventory business, and almost everything interesting about them follows from that: pricing is a daily auction, load factor is the master dial, and a small change in revenue or fuel swings profit by a lot.

The other defining fact is how little is left at the end. IATA, the global airline trade body, forecast in June 2026 that the industry will earn $23.0 billion of net profit on $1.165 trillion of revenue, a 2.0% net margin and about $4.50 for each passenger carried. That forecast was cut roughly in half after the Middle East conflict pushed up jet fuel; before the shock, IATA had projected $41 billion. IATA also notes that the industry has never posted a net margin above 5%. So the question for any airline is not how to get rich, but how to stay solidly above zero through the cycle.

Most revenue is still the ticket. Air Canada's 2025 annual report shows C$22,372 million of operating revenue, of which passenger revenue was C$19,604 million (87.6%, computed), cargo C$1,033 million (4.6%, computed) and other revenue C$1,735 million (7.8%, computed). Across the whole industry, IATA expects 2026 revenue of $839 billion from passenger tickets, $165 billion from ancillary items such as bags and seat selection, and $162 billion from cargo. Ancillaries are growing fastest, at 12.6%, against 9.2% for tickets.

The more telling story is inside the ticket and beside it. Delta's second-quarter 2026 release splits its $19.8 billion of revenue in detail. Premium tickets brought in $6.9 billion and main-cabin tickets $6.85 billion, so premium cabins are now slightly larger than economy as a share of revenue (35.0% against 34.7%, computed). Delta also reports that revenue streams other than main-cabin tickets (premium, loyalty, cargo, maintenance and so on) are 61% of its adjusted revenue, up from 59% a year earlier. Its refinery line is an odd extra: $2.1 billion of third-party fuel sales that carry matching cost, so it inflates revenue without adding much profit.

The loyalty programme is the part that behaves least like an airline. Delta received $2.4 billion from American Express in the quarter, up 16%. The card issuer pays the airline for points that it then hands to cardholders, so the airline is selling a financial product, not a seat. Air Canada's Aeroplan works the same way, and Air Canada used proceeds from an Aeroplan transaction to repay C$1.7 billion of debt and fund a C$800 million share buyback, according to its Q3 2026 release. The release does not disclose the transaction's size, so treat this as evidence of the programme's value, not a number to extrapolate from.

Cargo is a smaller but useful stream. Air Canada's cargo revenue was up 33% in Q3 2026, and Delta's grew 39% in Q2, but both are well under 5% of revenue at these carriers, so cargo helps at the margin rather than defining the model.

Start with the cost stack. Air Canada's 2025 expenses total C$21,454 million. The largest lines are wages, salaries and benefits at C$5,005 million (23.3% of costs, computed) and aircraft fuel at C$4,731 million (22.1%, computed). Next come depreciation (C$2,012 million), airport and navigation fees (C$1,587 million), aircraft maintenance (C$1,343 million), sales and distribution (C$1,075 million), ground packages (C$872 million) and regional capacity purchase fees (C$863 million). Operating income was C$918 million, a 4.1% operating margin (computed). That is a normal year for a good airline.

The industry view from IATA is similar but fuel-heavy in 2026. Total operating expenses are forecast at $1.117 trillion, of which fuel is $350 billion (31.4%, up from 25.4% in 2025) and labour is $271 billion (about 24%, computed). Non-fuel costs are growing a modest 4.0%, while fuel is up nearly 40%. IATA's assumptions explain why: Brent crude averages $95 a barrel (against $69 in 2025), jet fuel averages $152 a barrel (against $90), and the gap between jet fuel and crude, the crack spread, is at a historic high of $57 a barrel. Only about one-third of 2026 fuel use is hedged.

The Air Canada quarter shows what that does to a P&L. In Q3 2026, revenue rose 21% to C$6,984 million, yet operating income was only C$261 million, a 3.7% margin against 4.9% a year earlier. Fuel cost C$2,118 million, which is C$906 million more than a year ago and about 30% of revenue (computed). Fuel cost per litre rose to 148.3 cents from 88.3 cents. The fuel increase alone was about 3.5 times the quarter's operating income (computed). Management responded by cutting its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to C$2.4 to 2.7 billion from C$2.9 to 3.2 billion, and said that only about 70% of extra Q4 fuel cost would be recovered through fares and surcharges.

Delta shows the same pressure with a stronger starting point. Its September quarter operating margin was 7.2% on a GAAP basis (9.4% adjusted), and it says it has absorbed about $6 billion of higher fuel cost in 2026. Smaller, leisure-heavy Air Transat is on the sharp end: its fiscal third quarter to July 31 produced a C$106.6 million loss, with about C$105 million of extra fuel cost in the quarter, and it said its ability to pass costs to customers had been very limited. Ottawa has stepped in with federal financing for Transat and a federal loan for Porter.

Behind these costs is a supply problem. IATA says aircraft are scarce: the order backlog hit 18,100 in May 2026, more than half the active fleet, lease rates are at record levels, and older planes cost more to maintain. That is why airlines cannot simply grow their way out. Fewer planes keep competitors honest on capacity, but they also keep costs high.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The number is load factor: the share of seats that carry a paying passenger. Because the cost of flying is mostly fixed, the last few seats filled drop almost straight to profit, and the last few left empty are pure loss. IATA expects a record 84.0% industry load factor in 2026. Air Canada's was 89.1% in Q3 2026, up 2.6 points, in the peak summer quarter.

Load factor cannot be read alone, because an airline can fill a plane by selling cheap. The partner number is yield, the revenue earned per passenger-mile flown. Air Canada's yield rose 11.0% to 23.8 cents in Q3, so it filled more seats and charged more per mile at the same time, which is the combination that pays for a fuel shock. The summary is revenue per available seat-mile (roughly load factor times yield) set against cost per available seat-mile. Air Canada's Q3 unit revenue was 23.4 cents against a GAAP unit cost of 22.5 cents, which leaves a thin gap. Excluding fuel and one-off items, its adjusted unit cost was 14.45 cents, up only 3.3%, which shows that the squeeze came almost entirely from fuel.

That thin gap is why airlines obsess over capacity discipline. When one carrier adds seats on a route, rivals match, fares fall and everyone's load factor-yield trade-off worsens. In the autumn of 2026, Canadian commentators were already predicting a price war once the summer peak faded, with some smaller carriers at risk, which is a live example of the problem.

The most mature use of AI in aviation is revenue management: algorithms that decide, flight by flight and hour by hour, how many seats to sell at each fare bucket and when to raise prices. This directly attacks the master dial, because a one-point gain in load factor or yield is worth more than most cost programmes. Close behind are crew and fleet scheduling tools that re-plan a network when weather or a strike hits, and predictive maintenance that flags parts before they fail, which matters when older aircraft are being flown longer. Airport self-service and automated customer messaging take out some sales and service labour.

These tools help at the edges, but IATA's own numbers show the limits. Labour costs are forecast to rise 4.0% in 2026 while workforce productivity per employee falls 0.4%, because airlines are flying older fleets with fewer new aircraft and tight crew supply. Fuel, the biggest swing cost, cannot be automated away. For a consultant, the right question is not whether AI saves cost, but whether it raises revenue per seat or protects reliability enough to matter against a fuel bill that moved by hundreds of millions of dollars in one quarter.

Profit pools are uneven. Within the industry, IATA expects North American airlines to earn $9.4 billion in 2026 (a 2.5% net margin and $8.10 per passenger), down from $12.4 billion in 2025. That is better per passenger than the global $4.50, which tells you that scale, strong home markets and premium and loyalty revenue help. Outside the airlines, the owners of scarce things also do well: aircraft lessors at record lease rates and card issuers that pay for loyalty points sit in structurally healthier positions than the airline itself.

Concentration shapes who can pass costs on. In Canada, the Competition Bureau describes the domestic market as highly concentrated with two leading carriers. A June 2025 summary put Air Canada and WestJet at 56% to 78% of domestic passengers at the eight busiest airports, with a figure of up to 78% on key routes. Air Canada competes with WestJet on about 61% of its routes, down from 72% in 2019, and the bureau estimates one more competitor on a route is associated with 9% lower prices. Two dominant carriers can pass fuel costs on more easily than a sector of many small ones, but the Air Transat and Porter cases show that smaller, leisure-focused or less diversified carriers hit trouble first.

The cycle is the other half of the story. Airline profits move with GDP, consumer confidence and fuel. IATA's 2025 numbers (net profit of $45 billion on a 4.2% margin) were described as thin even in a good year, and 2026 halved them within a few months. Counter-cyclical cushions exist but are small: cargo, loyalty income that arrives whether or not planes are full, and sale-leasebacks, which Air Canada is using to raise cash (C$501 million so far in 2026, with an assumed C$1 billion for the year). Air Canada ended Q3 with C$8,018 million of liquidity and net debt of 1.3 times EBITDA, which is the kind of cushion that decides who survives a bad winter.

The counter-intuitive fact is that the industry earns less than its cost of capital even in good years. IATA puts 2026 return on invested capital at 4.3%, against a weighted average cost of capital of 8.5%, so the industry as a whole is destroying value by its own measure even while it reports a profit. The carriers that beat that gap do it by acting less like airlines and more like diversified businesses: Delta's premium cabins and American Express income, Air Canada's Aeroplan, cargo and maintenance work.

In a case interview you could say: an airline is a fixed-cost, perishable-seat business with a margin of a few percent, so it wins by filling planes at good prices, selling premium cabins and loyalty points, and staying liquid enough to survive the next fuel spike.

items.title: How Aritzia works
items.body: Aritzia designs its own clothes, has them made by outside factories and sells them mostly at full price through large boutiques and its own website. Sales rose 44.1% to $1.17 billion last quarter, and two-thirds now come from the US.
items.summary: Aritzia's second quarter of fiscal 2027 brought $1.17 billion of revenue, up 44.1%, and a 21.0% adjusted EBITDA margin. Here is how a Vancouver fashion brand makes its money, why new stores are the engine, and why sales per square foot matters more than the number of boutiques.
items.ai: Little AI is disclosed; the visible automation is RFID stock tracking and a robotics-enabled distribution centre in Delta, British Columbia.
items.caseq: Aritzia plans to double revenue in five years, mostly by opening US boutiques. How would you test whether the plan will work, and what could go wrong?
items.caseAnswer: Structure by revenue growth = (number of boutiques x productivity per boutique) + digital, then check margin and capital. (1) New-store productivity: compare each opening cohort's sales per square foot and payback with the company's claim of under 12 months; test whether newer US markets are performing as well as early ones. (2) Digital halo: measure how much online sales rise in a market after a boutique opens (company says about 65%) and whether that is incremental. (3) Margin: full-price sell-through, markdown rate by category, tariff and currency exposure, and whether adjusted gross margin can keep rising after the Q2 jump. (4) Capital and supply chain: return on about $1.1 billion of planned store space and $500 million for US distribution, with robotics at Delta. (5) Brand risk: category expansion into handbags, shoes and beauty could dilute the brand. Then size each lever, run downside cases on US comps and the Canadian dollar, and recommend a staged rollout with gates on productivity.

items.cs: Apparel retailers weighing store expansion, tariff exposure, inventory risk and omnichannel investment need growth-strategy, supply-chain and store-economics work.

paras: Aritzia is a Vancouver-based women's fashion brand that designs nearly everything it sells, has it made by outside factories, and sells it through its own boutiques and its own website and app. About 97% of net revenue comes from its exclusive brands, such as Aritzia, Wilfred, Babaton, TNA and The Super Puff, according to its annual information form for the year ended March 1, 2026. It sits at what it calls an attainable price point, between fast fashion and luxury. All dollar figures below are Canadian unless stated.

The master question for this piece is where the profit actually comes from. The answer is not clothing in general. It is full-price sales of a tightly edited, in-house range, sold through a small number of large, well-placed stores that also pull customers online. If the boutiques stopped selling, much of the profit would go with them, because the company says about half of boutique transactions are preceded by a digital interaction and opening a store in a new market lifts online sales there by about 65% on average.

The latest numbers show a machine running hot. In the 13 weeks ended August 30, 2026 (the second quarter of fiscal 2027), net revenue rose 44.1% to $1.17 billion, and comparable sales rose 34.5%. The United States was 66.6% of revenue, up 60.3%, while Canada grew 19.8%. The growth story is now mostly an American one.

Run the 60-second business-model test. Who pays, and for what? The customer pays, directly, for apparel and accessories. There is no advertiser, no marketplace take rate and no franchise royalty. Aritzia is a vertically integrated brand: the AIF says it controls design, merchandise planning, sourcing, production and retail for its exclusive brands. The only third-party product in the mix is a complement of premium denim, accessories and footwear.

Is revenue one-off or recurring? One-off, per purchase, so the real question is repeat behaviour rather than churn. The AIF says loyal clients who shop across channels spend three times more than single-channel clients. At the October 2026 investor day, management said digitally acquired customers are twice as likely to shop in both channels. That is the closest thing to a recurring engine here: a habit rather than a contract.

Is there a locked-in consumable? No. A coat or a pair of trousers can be bought elsewhere tomorrow, which is why the model leans on brand and scarcity instead. Who owns the assets? Mostly Aritzia, and that makes it asset-heavier than a typical brand. It runs company-operated distribution centres (Vaughan, Ontario at 550,000 sq ft, plus New Westminster, British Columbia), uses a third-party operator for Columbus, Ohio (560,000 sq ft), and is building a 380,000 sq ft site in Delta, British Columbia with planned robotics. It leases its boutiques, which average about 10,000 sq ft, and pays for the fit-out. Factories are outsourced: finished goods come from manufacturers in 15 countries, and the company does not hold long-term contracts with them.

The revenue engines, named plainly, are three. First, boutique retail: $766.9 million in Q2, up 34.1% and 65.6% of revenue. Second, digital, meaning the website and app: $402.9 million, up 67.7% and 34.4% of revenue. Third, a small tail of other brands and formats, including Reigning Champ men's wear (four boutiques, which Aritzia counts separately), plus a small food and beverage team. Over fiscal 2021 to 2026, ecommerce grew at a 25% compound annual rate, per the AIF.

What would break it? Four things: a tariff or duty shock on imported goods, a weak Canadian dollar against the US dollar, a fashion miss that leaves unsold inventory and forces markdowns, and a brand that loses its edge as it doubles in size. The AIF lists the first three as named risks. The fourth is the one a consultant should worry about most.

Start with the margin structure for the quarter. Reported gross profit was $667.4 million, a 57.1% margin, but that includes $97.4 million of refunds on tariffs paid earlier. Stripping those out, adjusted gross profit was $570.0 million, a 48.7% margin, up 490 basis points on a year earlier. Our arithmetic (computed): the refunds account for roughly 8.4 points of the reported margin, and about 15% of reported gross profit. Anyone quoting the 57.1% figure as the underlying run rate is wrong.

Below gross profit, selling, general and administrative costs were $345.4 million, 29.5% of revenue, compared with 30.8% a year earlier. Dollars rose 38.1%, but revenue rose faster, so the cost base was spread more thinly. That operating leverage is the heart of the profit story. Adjusted EBITDA reached $246.2 million, a 21.0% margin versus 15.2%. Net income was $201.7 million, but adjusted net income, which removes the refund effect and other items, was $156.0 million (computed difference: about $45.7 million). Diluted EPS was $1.70 as reported and $1.31 adjusted.

Why do margins rise when sales rise this quickly? Much of the cost is fixed per boutique, such as rent, a store manager and the fit-out, so extra sales fall mostly to profit. Fewer markdowns would also lift gross margin, though the filings reviewed give no markdown figure.

New stores carry the growth, and the claimed payback is unusually fast. At the investor day, management said new boutiques pay back in under 12 months, against a 12 to 18 month planning assumption. That is a company statement made in a presentation, so treat it as a claim to test rather than an audited fact. Over the past four years boutique count grew about 7% a year while square footage grew about 14% a year, which means the company is building bigger boutiques, not simply more of them. A planned four-level flagship of roughly 41,800 sq ft at Vancouver's CF Pacific Centre shows the direction.

The balance sheet is sound for a business that is growing this fast. Cash was $528.1 million at quarter end versus $352.3 million a year earlier. Inventory was $714.9 million, up 35.8%, which is slower than revenue growth of 44.1% (computed comparison). Capital spending was $62.4 million in the quarter, and the company guides to about $250 million for fiscal 2027.

Guidance frames the year. For fiscal 2027, revenue is expected at $4.78 billion to $4.88 billion, up roughly 29% to 32%, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of about 20.0% (17.8% in fiscal 2026). The plan assumes 12 to 13 new boutiques plus four to five repositions, with 11 to 12 of the new ones in the US. Q3 revenue is guided to $1.275 billion to $1.325 billion, up about 23% to 27%, which is a notable slowdown from Q2 and a reminder that the comparison base is getting harder.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: Many retailers watch same-store sales. For Aritzia, the number that explains the model is sales per unit of space, backed by how quickly a new boutique earns back its cost. The company does not publish sales per square foot in the documents we reviewed, so we cannot give that figure. What it does publish is the payback claim above, the 7% versus 14% growth gap between store count and square footage, and the Q2 comparable sales growth of 34.5%.

Here is why that matters. A boutique is a big fixed bet: long lease, fit-out, staff, and inventory. Its profit depends on how much merchandise moves through a square foot at full price. Management's plan shows it believes in bigger formats: it wants 5 to 7 repositions a year, where an old small store is replaced by a larger one in a better location, and it is shifting capital accordingly. Of roughly $2 billion of planned five-year capital spending, about $1.1 billion is for retail square footage, about $500 million for US distribution and about $400 million for technology, digital, offices and maintenance.

The strategic bet is that productivity per square foot can hold as the network expands from 146 boutiques today to something much larger. The fiscal 2032 target is $9.5 billion to $10.5 billion of revenue, a 15% to 17% compound growth rate, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of about 21%. Management expects US boutiques to reach 160 by fiscal 2032 from 87 at the end of fiscal 2027, and assumes comparable sales growth only in the low to mid single digits. In other words, today's 30-plus percent comps are not the plan; the plan relies on new space. If new stores open at lower productivity than the early winners, the whole arithmetic weakens. Management also expects the US to supply just over 85% of incremental growth, with Canada at about 5%.

Canada is being treated as mature. Management said the Canadian boutique count will decline slightly as legacy Wilfred, TNA and Babaton stores are folded into larger Aritzia boutiques, such as the Toronto Eaton Centre flagship opened in April 2026. That is a good example of how the metric guides decisions: fewer, bigger, better-placed stores.

Aritzia has said little in public about AI, and honesty requires saying so. The Q2 release and the five-year plan coverage we reviewed did not discuss AI. The AIF does carry a risk factor on AI and refers to reliance on third-party models. We make no claim about any payoff.

Where automation is visible, it is in the physical supply chain and inventory. First, Aritzia announced in December 2025 that it would deploy Nedap's RFID-based ID Cloud platform to get item-level stock accuracy, aimed at availability in stores and online and at ship-from-store, in-store pickup and returns. The coverage reported no measured results for Aritzia itself, so the benefits are expected, not proven. Second, the new Delta, British Columbia distribution centre is planned with robotics and increased automation, and the Ohio facility was slated for a retrofit in fiscal 2027.

Why does this matter for the economics? Digital revenue is growing at 67.7% and is a third of sales, and online orders cost more to pick, pack and return than boutique sales. Ship-from-store and buy-online-pick-up-in-store, which the AIF says most boutiques offer, only work if the stock count is right. RFID reduces the chance of promising an item that is not there. Better inventory visibility also supports the thing that drives margin: selling at full price with less excess stock to clear.

For a consultant, the useful question is where automation earns a return. In the warehouse, it pays when volumes are high and predictable, which is what the American push now promises: the plan puts about $500 million into US distribution. In design and the stores, the case is far less obvious, because the brand's value is a point of view and service. Automation here is a cost lever, not a moat.

Check the moat list. Brand is the main one: Aritzia has built a name that lets it hold prices well above fast fashion, and its exclusive-brand share of about 97% means no one else sells its product. Scale is a second, growing source of advantage, because bigger volumes spread design, distribution and marketing costs. Cost advantage is thin: it outsources production to many countries with no long-term contracts, so it has flexibility rather than a cost edge. There are no network effects, switching costs or regulation. Vertical integration is used where differentiation lives, in design and merchandise planning, and outsourced where it is commodity, in sewing.

The tariff episode shows both strengths and weakness. In fiscal 2026 the company moved some sourcing from China to Vietnam and Cambodia, a response only a company that controls its own sourcing can make. In Q2 it booked $97.4 million of refunds on tariffs paid earlier, which flattered reported profit. Guidance excludes any further refund benefit. The lesson is that the model passes through some of the risk but not all of it, so margins stay exposed to trade policy and to the Canadian dollar.

Who wins from here? Aritzia wins if US demand proves durable and each new boutique matches the productivity of earlier ones. Rivals in the premium women's wear segment face a competitor that is investing roughly $1.1 billion in new store space. The AIF says the Hill Shareholders held about 65.57% of voting power as of May 6, 2026, which supports long-term investment but limits outside shareholders' say.

The main risks are concentration and fatigue. Two-thirds of revenue comes from one country that was not the home market a decade ago; a few quarters of weaker comps would test the plan. A company that targets doubling its revenue and its client base also needs the product to keep feeling special. Expanding into handbags, shoes, jewellery and beauty, expected to add about $1.5 billion of revenue, widens the opportunity but dilutes focus. For consultants, a good engagement here would test new-boutique productivity by cohort, the markdown rate by category and the return on the distribution build-out.

In a case interview you could say: Aritzia is a vertically integrated brand that earns its profit by selling its own designs at full price through large boutiques that also drive online sales, so the business depends on how much each new square foot of store sells.

items.title: Porter's Five Forces: judging an industry before you judge a company
items.body: Five Forces tells you how much profit an industry's structure will let any firm keep. Here is the method, applied to Canadian grocery with the latest filings and regulator data.
items.summary: Rivalry, entry, substitutes, suppliers and buyers decide an industry's margin ceiling. We rate each force for Canadian grocery (Loblaw, Sobeys, Metro, Costco, Walmart) using Competition Bureau, company and Statistics Canada data.
items.ai: AI is good at gathering force-by-force evidence from filings and regulator reports, but it cannot decide which force matters most or what a firm should do about it.
items.caseq: A private-equity fund is considering buying a regional grocery chain in Canada. Using Five Forces, is the industry attractive?
items.caseAnswer: Verdict: moderately attractive, with regulatory risk. 1) Rivalry: few large players, cushioned, but fighting on discount and promotions. 2) Entry: barriers high (sites, scale, property controls) but policy is lowering them. 3) Substitutes: low in the category, but shoppers trade down inside it. 4) Suppliers: mixed; large brands matter, the Grocery Code of Conduct is in force. 5) Buyers: individually weak, collectively influential, price-aware and loyalty-card holders. Then: check the target's position (format, region, discount exposure) and what would change a force.

items.cs: Case-interview use: open an 'is this market attractive?' question by naming the five forces, rating each with one fact, and ending with a verdict.

paras: Porter's Five Forces is a way to judge how attractive an industry is, before you judge any one company in it. Michael Porter's argument is that profit is not only about how well firms run themselves. It is also about the structure around them. Five pressures decide how much of the value an industry creates is kept by the firms inside it, and how much leaks away to others.

The five forces are: rivalry among existing competitors; the threat of new entrants; the threat of substitutes; the bargaining power of suppliers; and the bargaining power of buyers. Strong forces squeeze profit, weak forces protect it. The output is a verdict on the industry's margin ceiling, which is why the framework sits in the strategy toolkit: it tells you whether the game is worth playing, and which part of the game to play.

The master question for this piece is: why would this business still be winning in ten years? Five Forces answers the first half. It shows what the industry will let any player earn, and which forces a player could change by its own choices.

Start by drawing the boundary. An industry is a set of firms whose products customers treat as close substitutes, in a defined geography. 'Food' is too wide. 'Supermarkets and supercentres in Canada' is workable, and you may need to split it further, for example into hard discount and full-service, because the forces differ by segment.

Then take each force and ask a specific question, with evidence. Rivalry: how many players are there, how similar are they, and do they compete on price or on something else? Entry: what would a newcomer need (capital, sites, supply chain, brand) and could incumbents block it? Substitutes: what else solves the same need, such as meal kits, restaurants or online delivery? Supplier power: do a few suppliers control something you cannot do without, or can you switch? Buyer power: are customers concentrated or able to switch cheaply?

Rate each force as low, moderate or high, and write the one fact that justifies the rating. This is where most analyses fail: a force is not 'high' because it sounds threatening, it is high because a number or a mechanism shows it. Look for facts like market shares, switching costs, share of costs a supplier represents, and the fixed-cost base that makes rivals fight for volume.

Finally, look at direction and at what is changing. Five Forces is a snapshot, so ask which force is moving, who or what is moving it (technology, regulation, a new entrant) and what that does to the margin ceiling. Many analysts also add a sixth lens, complementors or government, because regulation can reshape a force directly. We will see that in grocery.

Our industry is Canadian grocery retail. The Competition Bureau's 2023 market study found that most Canadians buy groceries from one of five companies: Loblaw, Sobeys (owned by Empire), Metro, Costco and Walmart. It reported that Loblaw, Sobeys and Metro each had more than 1,000 stores, including franchised ones, and that Costco and Walmart together had about 500. A 2026 Bureau update repeats that five-company finding.

Rivalry: moderate to high on the surface, but cushioned. Rivals are few, which usually dampens price wars. Yet they fight hard on value. Loblaw said in its second-quarter 2026 release (quarter ended June 20, 2026) that its discount banners again outperformed, and it opened 7 hard discount stores in the quarter. Empire's food same-store sales grew 1.2% in its quarter ended August 1, 2026, and it is rolling out its FreshCo discount banner in Atlantic Canada. Competition has moved to the discount aisle, and to promotions. Loblaw's September 2026 capital plan notes that the share of grocery sales bought on promotion has risen four percentage points since 2022.

New entrants: low to moderate threat. The Bureau pointed to property controls, which are clauses in leases or deeds that stop a rival grocer using a site, as a barrier that blocks new stores. It also noted that capital needs, low population density and the grocers' ownership of many discount banners make standalone entry hard. Policy is now pushing the barrier down: Manitoba passed a law barring new restrictive covenants in grocery, and the Bureau reports Sobeys, Loblaw and Walmart Canada have taken steps to remove such controls. Entry is not impossible, though. The Bureau lists online grocers as an area of innovation, and Retail Insider reports T&T planning new Ontario and Manitoba stores for 2028.

Substitutes: low to moderate. Restaurants, meal kits and delivery compete for some meals, but groceries are a necessity and most spending is hard to substitute. The real substitution happens inside the category, as shoppers trade down. Statistics Canada reports grocery prices rose 1.7% year over year in September 2026, the smallest annual increase since May 2024, but are still up 33.0% since September 2020. That cumulative rise is why shoppers move to discount banners and store brands.

Supplier power: mixed. For large national brands, the big grocers are crucial customers, and the Bureau noted that they receive supplier payments for shelf placement that independents generally do not. But suppliers are often large too. The relationship was serious enough that the industry built a Grocery Code of Conduct, which took full effect on January 1, 2026. It was prompted by supplier fees introduced by Walmart Canada and Loblaw in 2020, according to the Canadian Press. By July 2026 it had received 14 complaints, and 200 businesses had signed on, including all major grocers, though only a few hundred of the few thousand suppliers had. Read this as a sign that supplier power is strong enough to matter, and weak enough in some segments that a code was needed.

Buyer power: low per shopper, but price-aware. A single shopper has no leverage. But shoppers can switch. In the Bureau's 2023 survey, 79% said they visit multiple stores at least sometimes to find the best price, and 75% hold a loyalty card. Loyalty cards raise switching costs. Collectively, buyers also have political power: affordability is why Parliament and regulators keep returning to this sector.

The verdict: the industry structure supports healthy but politically exposed profits. The Bureau reported that the three biggest grocers' combined profit rose from about $2.4 billion in 2019 to $3.6 billion in 2022 (about 50%, computed). Loblaw alone earned $1,994 million of the $3,589 million in 2022 (about 56%, computed from the Bureau's table). Loblaw's retail gross margin in Q2 2026 was 32.2%, and its return on equity was 27.2% according to MarketBeat's summary of the earnings call. Those are strong figures. They are exactly what the forces predict: few rivals, high entry barriers and a necessity product. The caveat is that the Bureau said it could not obtain complete food-only margin data, so net margin conclusions need care.

A Five Forces grid is only useful if it leads to choices. The standard move is to ask, for each force, how a firm could weaken it or position itself where it is weakest. Think of it as three plays: position the firm where forces are weakest, shift the forces in its favour, or exploit change before others do.

Take Loblaw. The strongest pressure on margin is buyers moving to value. Its response, from its own releases, is to build the discount position itself: the 2026 plan puts about $2.4 billion into capital spending, with grocery expansion focused mainly on No Frills and Maxi. That keeps price-sensitive shoppers inside its own network, which reduces rivalry's bite. A discount store that you own cannot take sales from you.

Take Empire. The same logic explains rolling FreshCo into Atlantic Canada. It also explains the scale of its fiscal 2027 plan: Retail Insider reports a target of more than 25 new stores and roughly $850 million of capital spending, about half for renovations and store development.

Take a challenger, such as a regional independent or foreign entrant. Five Forces says the barrier is sites and supply, so the choice is where to enter: places where property controls are being removed, formats where scale matters less, or a niche such as ethnic grocery. Take a supplier: the code of conduct is a chance to strengthen its position by joining and documenting practices.

For the policy-maker, the framework points at the weakest link. If entry is the force that most protects profit, then the Bureau's recommendations make sense: ban property controls, back unit pricing so buyers can compare, and support new grocery models. Notice that the Bureau's September 2026 update says progress is partial and urges governments to adopt all four recommendations.
The first mistake is drawing the industry too wide or too narrow. Analyse 'retail' and every force looks mixed. Analyse one banner and you miss the competition inside the same parent company.
The second is treating the framework as a list of threats. Each force needs a rating and a fact. 'Rivalry is intense' with no evidence is the Five Forces version of a bland SWOT bullet.

The third is forgetting that a force can be high and the industry still profitable. Rivals may be many but disciplined, or the force may fall on someone else in the chain. Always ask who captures the value, and whether firms can pass costs on. Grocery shows this: costs rose, prices rose, and profits held.
The fourth is ignoring dynamics: regulation, technology and a change in consumer habits can move a force within a few years. A static grid in a moving industry is stale.

The fifth is mixing the industry with the firm. Five Forces tells you what the industry will allow. Whether Loblaw earns more than the average depends on its own advantages, such as scale, private labels and loyalty data, which belong in a separate moat analysis. Finally, do not forget numbers: show a market share, a switching cost, or a margin, with its date and source, and label your own arithmetic as computed.

AI is useful at the evidence stage. It can pull store counts and margins from filings, summarise regulator reports, track price changes and flag when a force shifts, for example when a new discount banner opens in a region. That is hours of research cut to minutes.

AI also changes the forces themselves. Online ordering and delivery lower the barrier for some entrants and raise buyers' ability to compare prices. For incumbents, automation in warehouses and forecasting lowers costs, which is why Empire and Metro are restructuring e-commerce fulfilment, according to Retail Insider. Dynamic pricing and personalised promotions can sharpen rivalry but also shape how the Bureau sees competition.

What AI cannot do is judge. A model will happily call every force 'high' or invent a plausible market share. Check each figure against the source, decide which force is decisive, and write the recommendation. The people who do this well are rated on judgment, not on a pretty grid.

items.title: How trucking makes money (and why it barely does)
items.body: Freight is paid by the mile, but trucks often drive back empty. A huge, fragmented market of carriers, brokers in the middle and constant cost pressure means margins are thin.
items.summary: Running a truck cost a record $2.34 a mile in 2025, according to the industry's main benchmark. Rates have not kept pace, and a sixth of all miles earn nothing. Here is why the economics are so tight.
items.ai: load matching, route and fuel optimisation, and automated freight brokerage.
items.caseq: A 200-truck regional carrier makes a 2% margin. The owner wants it doubled in 12 months. What are your levers?

paras: Trucking moves most of the goods in North America, and it is a business of very small margins and very large numbers of players. Shippers (the manufacturers and retailers with goods to move) pay carriers (the companies that own the trucks) by the mile or by the load. Brokers sit between them, matching loads to trucks and keeping a spread.

The basic problem is that the costs are mostly fixed or hard to control, while the price is set by supply and demand in an open market. When there are more trucks than freight, rates fall below what it costs to run them, and carriers keep driving anyway because a parked truck still has a payment due.

A carrier earns revenue per loaded mile, under either a contract with a shipper (a rate agreed for a year or so) or on the spot market (a price for a single load, set daily). Contract rates give stability; spot rates swing with demand and tend to run below costs when the market is weak.

The numbers show how tight things have been. FreightWaves, drawing on ATRI and its own SONAR rate data, reports that contract linehaul rates once cleared carriers' non-fuel costs by about $1.01 per loaded mile in 2022. By 2025 that cushion had shrunk to $0.26. Spot rates sat below non-fuel cost every year from 2023 to 2025. Dry van contract rates averaged $2.69 a mile in the third quarter of 2026, which FreightWaves says is below fourth-quarter 2021 levels, while non-fuel costs are about 30% higher than in 2021. In its view, the 2026 rate rise is a correction rather than a boom.

The industry benchmark is the American Transportation Research Institute's annual survey. Its 2026 edition, covering 2025, put the average cost of operating a truck at $2.336 per mile, up 3.4% and the highest in the report's history. Excluding fuel, costs rose 4.2% to $1.854 per mile.

The main lines: driver wages were about 82 cents per mile, with another 21 cents for benefits. Fuel was about 48 cents. Repair and maintenance rose 8.6% to 21.5 cents. Insurance was 10.6 cents per mile, up 3.9% in a year and 23.9% since 2021. Tariffs pushed tyre costs up 6.4% to about 5 cents. According to ATRI, only fuel and driver pay rose more slowly than inflation.
ATRI's previous report, covering 2024, found operating margins had fallen below 2%. Reading across both reports: a carrier that mismanages a few cents per mile can move from profit to loss.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The number is the share of miles driven empty. In ATRI's report on 2024 data, empty miles averaged 16.7%. Every empty mile still burns fuel, driver time and tyres but earns nothing.

A simple illustration: if a truck costs $2.34 per mile driven and 16.7% of miles are empty, the cost of each loaded mile is about $2.80 (2.336 divided by 0.833). Pricing a load at $2.50 a mile can therefore lose money even when it looks profitable. This is why carriers fight for backhauls, loads on the return leg, and why dense networks and repeat lanes beat one-off spot freight.

The most developed uses are digital freight matching (software that finds a load for an empty truck), route and fuel optimisation, and automated brokerage that prices and books freight without a phone call. Each of these targets the same issues: empty miles and brokers' spreads.
Autonomous trucks are a longer-term story and are not yet a material part of the economics. The nearer-term win for most fleets is data: knowing their true cost per mile by lane and by customer.

Winners are carriers with dense, repeat freight and low empty miles, those with strong contracts instead of spot exposure, and brokers with better pricing data. Losers are small fleets that cannot absorb a record insurance and maintenance bill.

Industry voices quoted by trade press describe 2026 as a turning point for freight rates, but also say costs are rising fast enough that fleets must keep cutting costs. For consultants, trucking is a clean example of a fragmented industry in which operational detail, not strategy slides, decides who survives.

items.caseAnswer: Start from the profit equation: margin equals revenue per mile minus cost per mile, divided by revenue per mile, so doubling a 2% margin to 4% needs roughly a 2% improvement in net revenue per mile. Levers, grouped MECE: (1) Revenue: shift mix from spot to contract, reprice the worst 10% of lanes, add accessorial charges (detention, layover), and raise rates on customers where the carrier's service is hard to replace. (2) Utilisation: cut empty miles by lining up backhauls and adding repeat lanes; each point of empty miles is worth about the same as a point of revenue. (3) Cost: fuel efficiency (idle time, speed, tyres), maintenance planning, insurance renegotiation and safety scoring, and driver retention to reduce turnover cost. (4) Overheads and capital: right-size the trailer-to-truck ratio and delay replacing old equipment. Prioritise by size and speed: empty miles and lane repricing first, because they need no capital and show results within a quarter. Validate with a cost-per-loaded-mile model by lane before acting.

items.title: How Chipotle runs a restaurant
items.body: Company-owned stores, a short menu and an assembly line built for speed. The economics come down to how many orders each store can push through at the lunch peak.
items.ai: digital ordering lanes, kitchen automation, and AI tools that tell crews what to cook and when.
items.caseq: Chipotle wants to raise throughput 10% without adding staff. What are your levers?
items.summary: Chipotle sells about $3.3 billion of burritos and bowls a quarter from more than 4,100 restaurants it owns itself. Here's how the machine works, where the money goes, and why the whole business comes down to one number: entrées per peak 15 minutes.

paras: Chipotle is a fast-casual chain with a deliberately simple model: a short menu of burritos, bowls, tacos and salads, assembled in front of the customer on a single production line. Unlike McDonald's or Subway, it doesn't franchise. It owns and operates every restaurant it runs in North America and Europe, which means it keeps all of each store's profit, but also carries all of its costs and risks.

That choice shapes everything. A franchisor earns royalties and lets franchisees worry about labour and food costs. Chipotle earns the full margin on every bowl, so its results move directly with how efficiently each restaurant runs. When things go well, the economics are excellent. When costs rise or traffic falls, there's no franchisee to absorb the hit.

Almost all revenue is food and drink sold in its own restaurants. In the third quarter of 2026, total revenue rose 9.6% to $3.3 billion. Most of that growth came from opening new restaurants, with a smaller boost from existing ones: comparable restaurant sales (stores open at least 13 months) rose 2.1%, made up of a 1.3% higher average bill and 0.8% more transactions.

That split matters. Growth from new stores is predictable but capital-hungry. Growth from more customers in existing stores is the healthiest kind, because it spreads fixed costs over more sales. Chipotle had a rough 2025: comparable sales fell 1.7% and customer counts fell 3.2%, its first full-year decline in over 20 years. Q3 2026 was its third straight quarter of rising transactions, which is why investors cheered. The shares jumped about 9% the day after the results.

Digital orders through the app, website and delivery platforms made up 38.8% of food and beverage revenue in the quarter, up from 36.7% a year earlier. Its loyalty programme, relaunched in April, now accounts for over a third of sales.

The key profitability measure is restaurant-level operating margin: revenue minus the direct costs of running restaurants (food, packaging, labour, rent and other operating costs). In Q3 2026 it was 23.3%, down from 24.5% a year earlier.

Where each dollar goes, roughly: food, beverage and packaging took 29.5% of revenue, and labour took 25.7%, up from 25.2% as wages rose. The rest covers occupancy and other operating costs before the margin. Beef and freight costs pushed food costs up, while menu price increases helped offset them.

Each restaurant does about $3.1 million in sales a year on a trailing basis, according to industry tracking of Chipotle's average restaurant sales. New restaurants are a big part of the story: management has said new stores deliver about 60% cash-on-cash returns in their second year, which is why it keeps opening one almost every day.

sections.h: The number that runs the business: throughput
paras: Because Chipotle sells most of its food in a few busy hours, the real constraint isn't demand. It's how many people a restaurant can serve during the lunch and dinner rush. The company measures this as entrées per peak 15 minutes. Every extra entrée served at peak is almost pure profit, because rent, staff and equipment are already paid for.

That's why most of Chipotle's strategy targets speed: a second, dedicated makeline for digital orders; the Chipotlane (a drive-through lane for pre-paid app orders, now in roughly 80% of new restaurants); and a high-efficiency equipment package that it says adds more than two extra entrées during the peak 15 minutes in restaurants that have it.

Chipotle is attacking throughput with a mix of AI and robotics. Its AI-enabled 'Cook to Needs' tool, which forecasts what to cook and when, went from pilot to more than 500 restaurants within the third quarter of 2026.

On the robotics side, it has tested an automated makeline built by Hyphen that assembles bowls and salads for digital orders underneath the counter, and the 'Autocado', which cuts, cores and peels avocados for guacamole. Bowls and salads make up roughly two-thirds of digital orders, which is why automating them could free staff to focus on the front line.

Rivals are racing too: Sweetgreen built its own automated 'Infinite Kitchen', and Cava has invested in Hyphen. For consultants, this is the classic operations question: where does automation raise capacity enough to pay for itself, and where does it just add cost and complexity?

Chipotle's advantages are scale, a simple menu that's easy to run consistently, a strong digital and loyalty base, and the discipline of owning every store. Its risks are the flip side: labour inflation hits it directly, food-safety incidents hurt the whole brand at once, and price increases can push away customers if they go too far.

The next growth chapter is international, with partner-operated restaurants in markets such as Mexico and the Middle East. It lets Chipotle grow abroad without carrying all the risk of building in unfamiliar markets itself. The 2026 plan calls for 350 to 370 new restaurants, including 10 to 15 international partner-operated ones.

items.caseAnswer: Structure it as capacity per peak 15 minutes = (orders the front line can make + orders the digital line can make) limited by the slowest step. Levers: (1) Labour deployment, not more labour: put the right people on the front line, digital line and grill at peak; the company has shown deployment alone can add several entrées per peak 15 minutes. (2) Remove bottlenecks: prep done before peak (prep failures cascade into slow lines), faster cooking equipment, automated avocado prep. (3) Shift demand: move orders to digital and Chipotlanes, which run in parallel with the front line. (4) Automate the digital line for bowls and salads (about two-thirds of digital orders). (5) Simplify: limit limited-time offers that slow the line. Then size each lever, check payback on equipment, and pilot in a few markets before rolling out.

items.title: SWOT analysis: how to make four boxes useful
items.body: Everyone has filled in a SWOT grid. Few people turn it into decisions. Here is how consultants use it, with Chipotle as a worked example.
items.summary: A SWOT lists strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Done badly it is a bland list. Done well it ranks what matters and ends in choices. We apply it to Chipotle, using its latest results.
items.ai: AI can draft a SWOT in seconds, but the draft is generic. Its best use is gathering evidence for each box, while people do the judging and ranking.
items.caseq: A regional grocery chain asks you for a SWOT analysis. What do you do before you draw the four boxes?

paras: A SWOT analysis sorts what is true about a business into four boxes. Strengths and weaknesses are internal: things the company controls or can change, like its brand, costs, people and processes. Opportunities and threats are external: things happening in the market that the company does not control, like customer trends, competitors, regulation and input prices.

The framework is popular because it is simple, and that is also its weakness. A grid of generic bullets (strong brand, rising competition) tells a client nothing they did not know. A SWOT earns its place only when every item is specific, backed by a number, ranked by importance, and connected to a decision.

Start with a question, not a grid. A SWOT of the whole company is rarely useful; a SWOT for a decision, such as whether to open in a new country or add automation, is. The question decides which facts matter.

Then use one test to sort every item: could the company change it next year? If yes, it is internal (a strength or weakness). If no, it is external (an opportunity or threat). Most mistakes come from putting an outside trend, like rising wages, into the weakness box.

Attach evidence to every bullet: a figure, a date and a source. Then rank each box by two things, how much it could move the results and how likely it is. Keep the top three or four in each box and drop the rest.

Chipotle's third-quarter 2026 results give plenty of evidence. Strengths: it owns all of its restaurants in North America, so it keeps the whole margin (23.3% restaurant-level margin in the quarter); digital orders are 38.8% of food and beverage sales; and its loyalty programme accounts for more than a third of sales. Its design is built around throughput, serving more people in the lunch rush.

Weaknesses: that same ownership means no franchisee to absorb cost increases. Margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3% in a year, and labour rose to 25.7% of revenue from 25.2%. The business also had a poor 2025, with comparable sales down 1.7% and customer counts down 3.2%, so it is recovering rather than cruising.

Opportunities: roughly 350 to 370 new restaurants planned for 2026, including 10 to 15 international partner-operated ones; drive-through Chipotlanes in about 80% of new restaurants; and automation such as the Cook to Needs forecasting tool, already in more than 500 restaurants, plus the robotic makeline and avocado machine being tested.

Threats: a food-safety incident would hit the whole brand at once; beef and freight costs push up food costs; further price increases could push customers away; and rivals such as Sweetgreen and Cava are building their own automation.

The step most people skip is turning the grid into strategy. A common method is a TOWS matrix, which crosses the boxes: use strengths to seize opportunities, use strengths to blunt threats, fix weaknesses that block opportunities, and protect against the combination of weaknesses and threats.

For Chipotle: its strong throughput and digital base (strengths) support rapid rollout of Chipotlanes in new stores (opportunity). Its exposure to labour inflation (weakness) is the reason automation (opportunity) matters. Its single-brand risk (threat) argues for a very high food-safety standard. Each crossing becomes a candidate strategy, which you then rank and assign an owner.
The deliverable is not the grid. It is a short list of prioritised moves, each tied to evidence.

The usual failures are generic bullets with no numbers, mixing internal and external factors, listing 20 items per box, treating every item as equal, and stopping at the list. A related error is using a SWOT as the whole analysis: it organises facts but does not size markets, test economics or compare options. It works best as a summary step after real research.

Another trap is looking only at the company's own point of view. A strength matters only relative to competitors: a loyal customer base is a strength if rivals lack one, and table stakes if they all have it.

AI tools will draft a SWOT in seconds, and the result is usually fluent but generic. Their useful role is evidence gathering: pulling figures from filings, summarising earnings calls and spotting competitor moves. The judgment, which items matter and what to do about them, is still the consultant's job, and it is where the value is.

items.caseAnswer: Before drawing anything, clarify the decision the client faces (for example, whether to fund a new format, enter a new region or cut costs) because that determines scope. Then gather evidence in three streams: internal data (store-level margins, shrink, labour cost, loyalty data), customer research (price perception, share of basket), and the market (competitor openings, discounters, supplier inflation, local regulation). Build the SWOT only after that, with every bullet carrying a number and a source and tested as internal or external. Rank by impact and likelihood, keep the top three per box, and cross them in a TOWS matrix to generate options. Present three to five prioritised strategic moves with owners, quick wins first, and note which assumptions need testing. Finally, challenge it: which strengths are real relative to competitors, and what would change the ranking?
